items.title: The Tipping Point: When Cyber Attacks Stop Being Limited by People
items.summary: For decades, the number and sophistication of cyberattacks were constrained by the people behind them. Skilled attackers were relatively rare, complex intrusions required experience, and investigating a failed attack often meant spending hours figuring out what went wrong. I think we have just crossed a threshold that fundamentally changes this situation. Over the past weeks, we have seen real-world attacks involving autonomous AI frameworks such as ARTEX and Cairn. These frameworks can plan significant parts of an intrusion, execute tools, evaluate their results and try alternative approaches when something fails. The human operator still provides objectives and may intervene, but no longer needs to direct every step. This capability is already being used in real attacks. And I think the consequences for the coming years will be substantial. Past / Now / Near Future — The AI Intrusion Tipping Point 1. Past: Attacks Were Limited by People For a long time, the attacker ecosystem had a fairly clear distribution of skills. At the bottom were large numbers of poorly skilled attackers running port scanners, public exploits, brute-force tools and Metasploit modules without necessarily understanding how they worked. When an exploit failed or a target behaved differently than expected, many simply moved on. A smaller group had enough technical knowledge to adapt existing tools, investigate vulnerabilities, develop scripts and carry out more complex intrusions. And then there was a relatively small group of highly capable operators who could develop sophisticated malware, discover or purchase exploits, evade security controls and maintain access to well-defended organizations for months. Of course, large-scale automated attacks existed long before AI. Botnets, vulnerability scanners and exploit frameworks could already target enormous numbers of systems. But the adaptive parts of complex intrusions still required considerable human expertise. Someone had to understand the results, choose the next step and troubleshoot unexpected problems. Human skill, time and attention remained important constraints. 2. Now: The Threshold Has Been Crossed For years, researchers experimented with combining LLMs and penetration-testing tools. Many early implementations were impressive demonstrations but struggled with complex tasks. They lost context, made mistakes, got stuck and required frequent human intervention. That has changed. Models have become capable enough, and orchestration frameworks mature enough, that agents can now perform substantial parts of real intrusions autonomously. Frameworks like ARTEX and Cairn make it possible to give an agent an objective, provide it with tools and let it explore possible attack paths. It can enumerate exposed services, investigate vulnerabilities, test credentials, execute commands, evaluate the results and try different approaches when something fails. The operator can monitor the process and intervene when necessary, but doesn’t have to make every decision. The important development is the combination of increasingly capable models, orchestration, persistent context and access to offensive tools. Open-weight models make this particularly interesting because attackers can operate their own infrastructure, modify models and combine them with custom skills without depending entirely on commercial AI providers. And we’re no longer talking about laboratory experiments. In September 2026, Gambit Security documented a campaign in which 105 Cairn attack projects were launched in five days, with at least 27 organizations compromised to varying degrees. Google, Mandiant, Microsoft and CrowdStrike have since documented additional real-world activity involving agentic offensive frameworks. Documented AI-driven Intrusions These attacks aren’t necessarily sophisticated or stealthy. They often use familiar techniques and generate plenty of recognizable activity. But the agents can work through failures and alternatives at a speed that previously required considerably more human effort. That is the threshold I believe we’ve crossed: autonomous attack execution has become operationally useful. 3. Near Future: The Economics of Cyberattacks Change What worries me most is what happens next. The average attacker doesn’t suddenly become a top-tier intrusion specialist. But someone with limited technical knowledge can now operate tools that make decisions and perform tasks previously requiring much more experience. Skilled operators, meanwhile, can automate large parts of their work and run more operations in parallel. These agents don’t need sleep, holidays or weekends. They can operate continuously, testing different approaches against different targets. As models become more capable and inference becomes cheaper, the cost of running these operations will likely continue to decrease. That changes the economics of an attack. What comes next — Organizations that previously weren’t attractive enough to justify hours or days of manual investigation may become worthwhile when they can be processed automatically. The attacker can investigate many more potential targets, concentrate effort where access appears promising and move on when the cost becomes too high. I’m particularly concerned about the implications for critical infrastructure. These environments often depend on complex, interconnected systems and software that cannot easily be replaced or updated. The ability to conduct many adaptive intrusions in parallel creates additional risks, even if the individual attacks rely mostly on familiar techniques. I actually expect AI to make software considerably more secure in the long run. Automated code reviews, testing and vulnerability discovery should help eliminate many common programming mistakes. But organizations have an enormous backlog of existing software to secure, while attackers can apply more capable models and tools to that software almost immediately. That’s why I expect the near future to be particularly difficult. The limiting factors for offensive operations are shifting. Human expertise and working hours still matter, but compute, infrastructure, available tools and the defenses encountered are becoming increasingly important. And unlike the speculative AI attack scenarios we’ve discussed for years, the operational capability behind this development is already here. The question is no longer whether AI agents can contribute to real intrusions. We have evidence that they can carry out substantial parts of them. What we don’t yet know is how quickly attackers will turn that capability into much larger, continuously operating campaigns. Sources and further reading Reports behind the campaign examples Gambit Security: Autonomous AI agents attacking online retailers — September 22, 2026. Investigation of a financially motivated campaign using Cairn, Strix and Hermes, reconstructed from recovered attacker infrastructure, agent records and evidence of compromise. CrowdStrike: Unknown Threat Actor Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Target South Korean Finance — October 7, 2026. Analysis of a campaign against financial organizations, including recovered ARTEX configurations, prompts and Claude Code session histories. Microsoft: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise — October 21, 2026. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX, including the ConnectWise-related activity and multiple intrusions reaching privileged cloud access in less than three hours. CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign — October 29, 2026. A separate operation targeting more than 200 organizations, with confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine. Broader context and analysis Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant: ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks — October 30, 2026. Observations of ARTEX, Cairn and Hexstrike during incident-response investigations, and analysis of the shift toward automated, adaptive intrusions. CrowdStrike: CrowdStrike Uncovers New Agentic AI Campaigns — October 21, 2026. Four additional actors using different agent configurations to make operational decisions and execute attacks, illustrating that this development extends beyond ARTEX and Cairn. Huntress: AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack — Analysis of rapid tooling changes, retry behavior and the limits of identifying AI involvement from victim-side telemetry alone. Framework documentation Cairn on GitHub — Project documentation for the general-purpose AI state-space search engine, initially validated through autonomous penetration testing. ARTEX Global Edition on GitHub — A public fork of ARTEX with architecture documentation and defensive guidance.

For decades, the number and sophistication of cyberattacks were constrained by the people behind them. Skilled attackers were relatively rare, complex intrusions required experience, and investigating a failed attack often meant spending hours figuring out what went wrong.

I think we have just crossed a threshold that fundamentally changes this situation.

Over the past weeks, we have seen real-world attacks involving autonomous AI frameworks such as ARTEX and Cairn. These frameworks can plan significant parts of an intrusion, execute tools, evaluate their results and try alternative approaches when something fails. The human operator still provides objectives and may intervene, but no longer needs to direct every step.

This capability is already being used in real attacks. And I think the consequences for the coming years will be substantial.

Past / Now / Near Future — The AI Intrusion Tipping Point1. Past: Attacks Were Limited by People

For a long time, the attacker ecosystem had a fairly clear distribution of skills. At the bottom were large numbers of poorly skilled attackers running port scanners, public exploits, brute-force tools and Metasploit modules without necessarily understanding how they worked. When an exploit failed or a target behaved differently than expected, many simply moved on.

A smaller group had enough technical knowledge to adapt existing tools, investigate vulnerabilities, develop scripts and carry out more complex intrusions. And then there was a relatively small group of highly capable operators who could develop sophisticated malware, discover or purchase exploits, evade security controls and maintain access to well-defended organizations for months.

Of course, large-scale automated attacks existed long before AI. Botnets, vulnerability scanners and exploit frameworks could already target enormous numbers of systems. But the adaptive parts of complex intrusions still required considerable human expertise. Someone had to understand the results, choose the next step and troubleshoot unexpected problems.

Human skill, time and attention remained important constraints.

2. Now: The Threshold Has Been Crossed

For years, researchers experimented with combining LLMs and penetration-testing tools. Many early implementations were impressive demonstrations but struggled with complex tasks. They lost context, made mistakes, got stuck and required frequent human intervention.

That has changed.

Models have become capable enough, and orchestration frameworks mature enough, that agents can now perform substantial parts of real intrusions autonomously. Frameworks like ARTEX and Cairn make it possible to give an agent an objective, provide it with tools and let it explore possible attack paths.

It can enumerate exposed services, investigate vulnerabilities, test credentials, execute commands, evaluate the results and try different approaches when something fails. The operator can monitor the process and intervene when necessary, but doesn’t have to make every decision.

The important development is the combination of increasingly capable models, orchestration, persistent context and access to offensive tools. Open-weight models make this particularly interesting because attackers can operate their own infrastructure, modify models and combine them with custom skills without depending entirely on commercial AI providers.

And we’re no longer talking about laboratory experiments. In September 2026, Gambit Security documented a campaign in which 105 Cairn attack projects were launched in five days, with at least 27 organizations compromised to varying degrees. Google, Mandiant, Microsoft and CrowdStrike have since documented additional real-world activity involving agentic offensive frameworks.

Documented AI-driven Intrusions

These attacks aren’t necessarily sophisticated or stealthy. They often use familiar techniques and generate plenty of recognizable activity. But the agents can work through failures and alternatives at a speed that previously required considerably more human effort.

That is the threshold I believe we’ve crossed: autonomous attack execution has become operationally useful.

3. Near Future: The Economics of Cyberattacks Change

What worries me most is what happens next.

The average attacker doesn’t suddenly become a top-tier intrusion specialist. But someone with limited technical knowledge can now operate tools that make decisions and perform tasks previously requiring much more experience. Skilled operators, meanwhile, can automate large parts of their work and run more operations in parallel.

These agents don’t need sleep, holidays or weekends. They can operate continuously, testing different approaches against different targets. As models become more capable and inference becomes cheaper, the cost of running these operations will likely continue to decrease.

That changes the economics of an attack.

What comes next —

Organizations that previously weren’t attractive enough to justify hours or days of manual investigation may become worthwhile when they can be processed automatically. The attacker can investigate many more potential targets, concentrate effort where access appears promising and move on when the cost becomes too high.

I’m particularly concerned about the implications for critical infrastructure. These environments often depend on complex, interconnected systems and software that cannot easily be replaced or updated. The ability to conduct many adaptive intrusions in parallel creates additional risks, even if the individual attacks rely mostly on familiar techniques.

I actually expect AI to make software considerably more secure in the long run. Automated code reviews, testing and vulnerability discovery should help eliminate many common programming mistakes. But organizations have an enormous backlog of existing software to secure, while attackers can apply more capable models and tools to that software almost immediately.

That’s why I expect the near future to be particularly difficult.

The limiting factors for offensive operations are shifting. Human expertise and working hours still matter, but compute, infrastructure, available tools and the defenses encountered are becoming increasingly important.

And unlike the speculative AI attack scenarios we’ve discussed for years, the operational capability behind this development is already here.

The question is no longer whether AI agents can contribute to real intrusions. We have evidence that they can carry out substantial parts of them. What we don’t yet know is how quickly attackers will turn that capability into much larger, continuously operating campaigns.

Sources and further readingReports behind the campaign examples

  • CrowdStrike: Unknown Threat Actor Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Target South Korean Finance — October 7, 2026. Analysis of a campaign against financial organizations, including recovered ARTEX configurations, prompts and Claude Code session histories.
  • Microsoft: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise — October 21, 2026. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX, including the ConnectWise-related activity and multiple intrusions reaching privileged cloud access in less than three hours.
  • CrowdStrike: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign — October 29, 2026. A separate operation targeting more than 200 organizations, with confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine.
Broader context and analysis

  • CrowdStrike: CrowdStrike Uncovers New Agentic AI Campaigns — October 21, 2026. Four additional actors using different agent configurations to make operational decisions and execute attacks, illustrating that this development extends beyond ARTEX and Cairn.
  • Huntress: AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack — Analysis of rapid tooling changes, retry behavior and the limits of identifying AI involvement from victim-side telemetry alone.

Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links. The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it. The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash Why Apple makes such good bait Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks. Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention. The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context. Apple Cash isn’t an Apple Gift Card The page blurs two different things: Apple Cash is money you send, receive and spend through Apple Wallet. An Apple Gift Card adds money to your Apple Account balance for Apple purchases. Apple warns that its gift cards can only be used for Apple purchases, and that someone asking you to pay them with one is probably a scammer. But neither Apple Cash nor an Apple Gift Card comes from a website that “unlocks” it after you install an app. The fake site leans hard on Apple’s name. It calls the app it promotes an “Official Apple Partner” that is “Verified by Apple Cash,” and its footer claims “Copyright © 2026 Apple Inc.” None of that is true. A “verification” that verifies nothing We looked at the code behind the page’s three steps: Eligibility Check, Verify Device and Claim Reward. The eligibility check is a timer. The four items that tick green, including “Location: United States,” are just labels that light up on a schedule. The page never checks where you are or what device you use. Everyone passes in under four seconds. It tells users to download an app for “device verification” The device verification is an app install. The page tell users to download an app called Reco Social, then tells them to create an account, and install and play a game. We found no evidence that Reco Social or its developer created or operated the fake reward page. When you tap Download & Open App , the page opens a link in a new tab. Five seconds later, it starts showing “Verifying device…”. Nothing is being verified. The page has no way of knowing whether you installed anything, created an account or played a game. The reward is the same link again. Ten minutes after you tap the button, the page moves on by itself and announces “Device Verified Successfully,” whether or not you installed anything. The Claim Your $750 button doesn’t add anything to your wallet. It opens the same link as the download button. Fake urgency The page is built to stop you from thinking too long: “Only 47 spots left today” always starts at 47. It drops by one every 30 seconds and stops at 3, so it never runs out. The “claimed $750” pop-ups are generated at random from a list of 15 first names and 15 US states, with a random “minutes ago.” Every visitor sees a new one every 8 to 15 seconds. The 10-minute “Session Expires” countdown doesn’t end anything when it hits zero. Who gets paid? The download button doesn’t go directly to the App Store. It first goes through a tracking link on taprkr[.]com. These links can be used in affiliate marketing to credit clicks and installs to whoever sent the traffic. The link carries a label, “recosocial-cpr.” CPR can stand for “cost per registration,” a deal where a promoter earns money when someone signs up. That label alone doesn’t confirm how this offer pays. The destination varied in our tests. The link led to an offer labeled “playful-rewards-revshare” on iPhone and an ad network on PC. A revshare (revenue share) deal usually pays the promoter a cut of what users later spend, such as on in-app purchases. The tracking labels suggest that promoters may earn money from registrations or spending in promoted apps, but they don’t confirm how this offer pays. Users don’t receive the promised $750. We have no evidence that Reco Social or any app at the end of these links is behind the fake Apple page. Deceptive affiliate promoters can send traffic to legitimate apps because they may earn money for installs or signups regardless of how users were persuaded. The page also loads a TikTok tracking pixel, which advertisers use to measure campaigns. This could mean the operators are measuring traffic from TikTok, but it doesn’t show where the link was shared. What’s the harm if it’s “just” an app install? Compared to a page that steals passwords or card numbers, this one can look harmless. But you still pay a price: You give away personal data. Creating an account means handing over your email address, phone number or social login to a service you only signed up for because of a lie. You may be encouraged to spend. Many mobile games make their money from in-app purchases, and with a revenue-share deal, someone profits when you spend. You may be set up for the next scam. Fake reward offers often come in chains. The next one may ask for your Apple Account details, card number, or a “small processing fee.” You lose time chasing a reward that was never coming. How to stay safe Keep these points in mind if you come across an Apple Cash or other Apple-related offer online: Don’t expect an app install to pay you in Apple Cash. Be suspicious of any “Apple” offer that asks you to download a third-party app, create an account or play a game to receive Apple Cash or an Apple Gift Card. Verify Apple Cash only in Settings. The real identity check is in Settings > Wallet & Apple Pay > Apple Cash . Treat any website or message that asks you to “verify” Apple Cash somewhere else as suspicious. Be extra careful around launches and holidays. iPhone Duo deals, giveaways and preorder offers will keep circulating. Go to apple.com or the Apple Store app yourself instead of following links. Check the address bar. Apple’s website is apple.com. A page on a domain like applecashgiftcard[.]com is not Apple, however much it looks like it. Treat countdowns and “spots left” as red flags. Fake urgency is there to rush you past the moment you’d ask, “Why would anyone give me $750 for this?” Already installed an app from a page like this? You didn’t earn a reward, so you can delete the app. Delete any account you created through it, cancel any subscriptions in your App Store settings, and change that password on any other accounts where you reused it. Never pay with gift cards, and never pay to receive a prize. As the FTC puts it, “No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.” If a “reward” asks for a fee, your card details or gift card codes, it’s a scam. Report it. Apple asks people to forward suspicious Apple-themed messages to reportphishing@apple.com. You can also report the ad or post to the platform where you saw it and, in the US, report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov . How Malwarebytes helps Malwarebytes can help block known scam pages. Use Browser Guard with a supported browser, or Web Protection in Malwarebytes for iOS when browsing with Safari. If you’re not sure whether a link, text or offer is real, you can ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you click. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. In this article
  • A fake $750 Apple Cash offer funnels users toward app and game promotions
  • Its device checks, countdown, and “spots left” claims aren’t real
  • Users get no reward and may share information or spend money in games

A page we found promises a $750 Apple Cash reward if you complete a quick “device verification.” There is no reward, and the page does not verify your device. Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links.

The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it.

The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash Why Apple makes such good bait

Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks.

Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention.

The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context.

Apple Cash isn’t an Apple Gift Card

The page blurs two different things:

  • Apple Cash is money you send, receive and spend through Apple Wallet.
  • An Apple Gift Card adds money to your Apple Account balance for Apple purchases.

Apple warns that its gift cards can only be used for Apple purchases, and that someone asking you to pay them with one is probably a scammer. But neither Apple Cash nor an Apple Gift Card comes from a website that “unlocks” it after you install an app.

The fake site leans hard on Apple’s name. It calls the app it promotes an “Official Apple Partner” that is “Verified by Apple Cash,” and its footer claims “Copyright © 2026 Apple Inc.” None of that is true.

A “verification” that verifies nothing

We looked at the code behind the page’s three steps: Eligibility Check, Verify Device and Claim Reward.

The eligibility check is a timer. The four items that tick green, including “Location: United States,” are just labels that light up on a schedule. The page never checks where you are or what device you use. Everyone passes in under four seconds.

It tells users to download an app for “device verification”

The device verification is an app install. The page tell users to download an app called Reco Social, then tells them to create an account, and install and play a game. We found no evidence that Reco Social or its developer created or operated the fake reward page.

When you tap Download & Open App, the page opens a link in a new tab. Five seconds later, it starts showing “Verifying device…”. Nothing is being verified. The page has no way of knowing whether you installed anything, created an account or played a game.

The reward is the same link again. Ten minutes after you tap the button, the page moves on by itself and announces “Device Verified Successfully,” whether or not you installed anything. The Claim Your $750 button doesn’t add anything to your wallet. It opens the same link as the download button.

Fake urgency

The page is built to stop you from thinking too long:

  • “Only 47 spots left today” always starts at 47. It drops by one every 30 seconds and stops at 3, so it never runs out.
  • The “claimed $750” pop-ups are generated at random from a list of 15 first names and 15 US states, with a random “minutes ago.” Every visitor sees a new one every 8 to 15 seconds.
  • The 10-minute “Session Expires” countdown doesn’t end anything when it hits zero.
Who gets paid?

The download button doesn’t go directly to the App Store. It first goes through a tracking link on taprkr[.]com. These links can be used in affiliate marketing to credit clicks and installs to whoever sent the traffic.

The link carries a label, “recosocial-cpr.” CPR can stand for “cost per registration,” a deal where a promoter earns money when someone signs up. That label alone doesn’t confirm how this offer pays.

The destination varied in our tests. The link led to an offer labeled “playful-rewards-revshare” on iPhone and an ad network on PC. A revshare (revenue share) deal usually pays the promoter a cut of what users later spend, such as on in-app purchases.

The tracking labels suggest that promoters may earn money from registrations or spending in promoted apps, but they don’t confirm how this offer pays. Users don’t receive the promised $750.

We have no evidence that Reco Social or any app at the end of these links is behind the fake Apple page. Deceptive affiliate promoters can send traffic to legitimate apps because they may earn money for installs or signups regardless of how users were persuaded.

The page also loads a TikTok tracking pixel, which advertisers use to measure campaigns. This could mean the operators are measuring traffic from TikTok, but it doesn’t show where the link was shared.

What’s the harm if it’s “just” an app install?

Compared to a page that steals passwords or card numbers, this one can look harmless. But you still pay a price:

  • You give away personal data. Creating an account means handing over your email address, phone number or social login to a service you only signed up for because of a lie.
  • You may be encouraged to spend. Many mobile games make their money from in-app purchases, and with a revenue-share deal, someone profits when you spend.
  • You may be set up for the next scam. Fake reward offers often come in chains. The next one may ask for your Apple Account details, card number, or a “small processing fee.”
  • You lose time chasing a reward that was never coming.
How to stay safe

Keep these points in mind if you come across an Apple Cash or other Apple-related offer online:

  • Don’t expect an app install to pay you in Apple Cash. Be suspicious of any “Apple” offer that asks you to download a third-party app, create an account or play a game to receive Apple Cash or an Apple Gift Card.
  • Verify Apple Cash only in Settings. The real identity check is in Settings > Wallet & Apple Pay > Apple Cash. Treat any website or message that asks you to “verify” Apple Cash somewhere else as suspicious.
  • Be extra careful around launches and holidays. iPhone Duo deals, giveaways and preorder offers will keep circulating. Go to apple.com or the Apple Store app yourself instead of following links.
  • Check the address bar. Apple’s website is apple.com. A page on a domain like applecashgiftcard[.]com is not Apple, however much it looks like it.
  • Treat countdowns and “spots left” as red flags. Fake urgency is there to rush you past the moment you’d ask, “Why would anyone give me $750 for this?”
  • Already installed an app from a page like this? You didn’t earn a reward, so you can delete the app. Delete any account you created through it, cancel any subscriptions in your App Store settings, and change that password on any other accounts where you reused it.
  • Never pay with gift cards, and never pay to receive a prize. As the FTC puts it, “No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.” If a “reward” asks for a fee, your card details or gift card codes, it’s a scam.
  • Report it. Apple asks people to forward suspicious Apple-themed messages to reportphishing@apple.com. You can also report the ad or post to the platform where you saw it and, in the US, report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
How Malwarebytes helps

Malwarebytes can help block known scam pages. Use Browser Guard with a supported browser, or Web Protection in Malwarebytes for iOS when browsing with Safari.

If you’re not sure whether a link, text or offer is real, you can ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you click.

items.summary_html:
A phishing kit called SkyW4lker (also branded SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel) is quietly taking over Microsoft 365 accounts without ever stealing a password.

Instead of cracking logins or breaking MFA, it tricks employees into approving a legitimate Microsoft device-code sign-in, handing attackers a valid session to corporate mailboxes, documents, and connected apps.

The kit has been active since June 2026 and is accelerating fast. Researchers at ANY.RUN tracked 618 sandbox analyses tied to SkyW4lker between June and October 21, 2026, with monthly submissions climbing from 20 in June to 200 in September.

Nearly half (46–47%) of those submissions came from the United States, more than twice the share of any other country.

For US enterprises running on Microsoft 365, that makes SkyW4lker one of the more pressing identity threats of the quarter.

This article breaks down how the kit works, who it targets, how it was traced back to a sibling phishing platform, and what SOC teams and security leaders can do about it.

Key takeaways
  • No password theft, no MFA bypass needed. SkyW4lker abuses Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 device-code flow. The victim types a code into a real Microsoft login page; the attacker gets the token.
  • Delivery looks like routine business. Password-protected PDF, DOCX, or XLSX attachments posing as contracts, invoices, statements, and service proposals, with the password in the email body.
  • Trusted platforms are part of the chain. Lure and redirect pages sit on Google Sites, Miro, Zoom, Smartsheet, Axure Cloud, Cloudflare R2, Linode object storage, and similar services, so links pass reputation checks.
  • The kit is professionally built. A PHP backend, obfuscator.io-style JavaScript, IP geolocation of every visitor, CAPTCHA gating to block scanners, and an admin panel with Telegram-based MFA and live victim notifications.
  • It shares DNA with Gabagool. Identical JavaScript modules, landing-URL formats, CAPTCHA widget, and hosting directories link SkyW4lker to the Gabagool credential-phishing kit active since April 2026. ANY.RUN assesses with high confidence that one developer built both.
  • US tech, manufacturing, and government organizations are the main submitters, followed by India, Canada, and the UK.
  • Faster correlation shortened the investigation. ANY.RUN’s Related Threat Context surfaced earlier sandbox sessions with the same URL patterns, which let analysts pivot into Threat Intelligence Lookup, expand the campaign cluster, and locate the kit’s admin panel.
What SkyW4lker is

SkyW4lker is a device-code phishing kit: it rents or sells attackers a complete pipeline for turning a phishing click into a working Microsoft 365 session. It first appeared on June 23, 2026 and has been continuously updated since, with new endpoints and changing URL tokens.

AttributeDetailThreat typePhishing kit (device-code phishing)ObjectiveMicrosoft 365 / OAuth access tokens, plus harvested emails, passwords, and MFA statusCore techniquesDevice-code abuse, obfuscated JavaScript (obfuscator.io), IP geolocation and ISP profiling, CAPTCHA gating (Cloudflare Turnstile and a self-hosted widget)DeliveryPassword-protected PDF/DOCX/XLSX/EML attachments; redirect links on Google Sites, Google Maps, Miro, Zoom, Smartsheet, Axure CloudLure themesContracts, invoices, approved statements, Fedwire payment notices, service proposalsHostingMostly DigitalOcean VPS (50 of 92 backend IPs), look-alike domains with Microsoft-themed subdomain chains, free dynamic-DNS hostsOperator / brandSkyW4lker (SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel)Activity windowJune 2026 – presentRelated kitGabagool (credential phishing, active since April 2026) Why US enterprises are in the crosshairs “SkyW4lker activity by country and sector, June–October 2026 (ANY.RUN data)”

The United States accounts for roughly 47% of all SkyW4lker-related sandbox submissions. The organizations submitting samples cluster in technology, manufacturing, and government, sectors where Microsoft 365 is the default collaboration layer and where a compromised mailbox can expose contracts, financial data, and supply-chain partners.

The risk is structural rather than technical. Device-code phishing succeeds against accounts that have MFA enabled, because the user genuinely completes an MFA-protected sign-in; they simply do it on the attacker’s behalf. That means four things for enterprise security:

  • Identity policy gaps. If device-code authentication is allowed broadly, MFA alone will not stop this attack.
  • Detection blind spots. Every step touches a legitimate service: a real document platform, a real CAPTCHA, a real Microsoft login page. Nothing in the chain looks obviously malicious to email filters or users.
  • Wide blast radius. One token can unlock Outlook, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and any app federated through Entra ID, and it becomes a launchpad for phishing customers and partners from a trusted address.
  • Higher response costs. Separating a malicious device-code sign-in from thousands of legitimate ones, then scoping what the attacker touched, consumes Tier-1 and Tier-2 time.

Protect corporate accounts from Microsoft 365 phishing attacks with faster detection and response. Talk to ANY.RUN about enterprise protection →

How a SkyW4lker attack unfolds

The full chain, from lure document to device-code prompt, was detonated and recorded in the ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox. You can replay it and pull indicators here: View the SkyW4lker analysis session →

“The password-protected PDF lure opened inside the ANY.RUN sandbox”
  1. The lure lands. The target receives an email about a commercial offer, contract, invoice, or confidential document. Attached is a password-protected PDF, DOCX, or XLSX; the password sits in the email body. The encryption defeats attachment scanning, and the password-in-body pattern feels normal to anyone who deals with vendors.
  2. The redirect chain. The document contains a link, usually to a CAPTCHA page. Some variants add an intermediate decoy page on Miro, Google Sites, Zoom, or a cloud bucket before forwarding the victim. The CAPTCHA (Cloudflare Turnstile or the kit’s own widget) keeps automated URL scanners from ever seeing the payload page.
  3. The device-code prompt. The victim arrives at a branded phishing page that displays a Microsoft device code and instructs them to enter it at Microsoft’s real login.microsoft.com/device page. Once they do, and complete MFA if prompted, the attacker’s backend receives an OAuth access token for the account. No password ever crosses the wire to the attacker, and the sign-in shows up in Entra ID as a legitimate device-code authentication.
“The device-code phishing page as rendered in the ANY.RUN sandbox” Inside the kit

The phishing page is a thin front end for a PHP backend, and ANY.RUN’s In-Browser Data Inspection exposes how it works by showing the live DOM and HTTP traffic side by side.

“Obfuscated JavaScript from the phishing page in the Browser Data view”

The main script loads helper modules, wires up the page’s buttons, and talks to the backend through one endpoint, /session_public.php, with two actions:

  • action=start sends the victim’s IP address, ISP, organization, and geolocation to the server and receives a session ID.
  • action=poll fires every few seconds with that session ID, asking whether the victim has finished authenticating. When the answer flips to yes, the attacker has the token.
“Repeated action=poll requests from the phishing page, visible in the sandbox network stream” ModuleWhat it doesclient_geo.jsFingerprints the visitor’s location via ip-api.com, ipapi.co, or ipwho.is (or a server-side client_geo.php). Used to profile targets and feed the admin dashboard.url_helper.jsUtility wrappers for building GET parameters and normalizing URLs.endpoint.jsTracks the victim’s state and logs email, password, browser, MFA status, and country to php/endpoints/accounts.php.

The JavaScript is obfuscated in obfuscator.io style; 520 of the 618 analyses carry ANY.RUN’s obfuscated-js tag.

That is deliberate friction for anyone trying to reverse the page statically, which is why detonating it in an interactive sandbox and watching the requests is the faster route.

From one URL to the whole campaign

Finding one SkyW4lker page is easy. Finding the other 170-plus domains, the shared hosting, the admin panel, and the sibling kit is where most investigations stall.

Traditionally that means repeated IOC lookups, manual correlation across old cases, and a lot of copy-pasting between tools.

ANY.RUN’s Related Threat Context feature collapsed that work. Inside the sandbox session, a Related analyses panel listed earlier submissions that used the same /session_public.php URL pattern, giving analysts an instant starting cluster instead of a blank search box.

“Related Threat Context surfacing earlier sandbox sessions with matching SkyW4lker URL patterns”

From there, a one-click pivot into Threat Intelligence Lookup on the distinctive endpoint returned additional phishing activity, expanded the campaign to its current size, and exposed infrastructure overlaps that would otherwise have taken days to assemble.

The same workflow applies to any suspicious URL or indicator a SOC receives: start from the alert, see what the community has already analyzed, and build on it rather than starting over.

“Threat Intelligence Lookup query on the unique /session_public.php endpoint”

The payoff shows up at both tiers. Tier-1 analysts spend less time re-researching indicators that someone else already resolved and get enough evidence to triage confidently.

Tier-2 analysts receive richer context up front and can focus on the cases that actually need deep analysis.

Give your SOC the context needed to speed up phishing investigations, reduce repetitive work, and boost Tier-1 productivity. See how the Interactive Sandbox connects threats →

The admin panel

Because each phishing page runs its own backend, the operator’s control panel usually lives on the same host.

Combining Threat Intelligence Lookup results with external data turned up a login form at /admin/index.php, and its stylesheet (command-center.css) describes what the kit offers its customers:

  • Operator login with MFA delivered over Telegram
  • A victim dashboard fed by client_geo.js geolocation data
  • Server management and generation of new phishing links
  • Real-time notifications whenever a target opens a link
“Login form of the SkyW4lker administration panel” “CSS class names revealing dashboard, server-management, and notification features” SkyW4lker and Gabagool: one developer, two attack modes

Searching ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence for SkyW4lker’s module paths (/js/client_geo.js, /js/url_helper.js, /js/endpoint.js) also returns sessions tagged Gabagool, a credential-phishing kit first seen on April 23, 2026, two months before SkyW4lker.

FeatureSkyW4lkerGabagoolFirst seenJune 23, 2026April 23, 2026Analyses in six months618458Shared JS modulesclient_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js (since July 2026)Same three modules (since late April 2026)Visit endpoint/assets/php/endpoints/confirm_visit.phpIdenticalSelf-hosted CAPTCHA/assets/private_captcha/public/widget.js?v=4IdenticalLanding tokenzt[A-Za-z0-9]{32}op, then it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us from Aug 10Same tokens, it…us from Aug 5Shared hosts and directories5200m[.]com/kvme2/, torvion[.]life/ofulium/, ghethim[.]com/hyllen/Same directories, within days of each otherHostingMostly DigitalOceanMostly DigitalOcean; shared IP 172.86.85[.]51Main endpointsession_public.php (device-code flow)accounts.php (username/password harvesting)

Some Gabagool sessions even load the kit from directories literally named skywalker and skyw4lker on goldcreekconcrete[.]com and goldcreekconcrete[.]org.

ANY.RUN’s assessment: the same developer built both kits, and they are best understood as two modes of one phishing platform, one that harvests passwords, one that harvests device-code tokens.

Whether a single operator runs both, or multiple customers bought the same product, the data cannot yet say.

How to detect SkyW4lker and reduce exposure For SOC analysts and threat hunters
  • Hunt the kit’s fingerprints. Alert on outbound requests to /session_public.php?action=start followed by repeated ?action=poll calls, and on the three module paths (client_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js) under /assets/js/. The landing token regex //it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us (previously //zt[A-Za-z0-9]{32}op) is a reliable signature for the landing URL.
  • Tie phishing to sign-ins. In Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs, filter for device-code authentications and correlate them against recent suspicious emails or document-share notifications to the same user. A device-code sign-in minutes after a “protected invoice” email is a strong compromise signal.
  • Detonate, don’t guess. Password-protected attachments and CAPTCHA-gated links defeat static scanners by design. Open them in an interactive sandbox, supply the password, pass the CAPTCHA, and watch the real traffic.
  • Pivot beyond the single IOC. Use Related Threat Context and Threat Intelligence Lookup to check whether the domain, endpoint, or module path already appears in other analyses. That turns a one-off alert into campaign-level visibility in minutes.
  • Scope the follow-on. When a token theft is suspected, review mailbox rules, OAuth app consents, SharePoint/OneDrive access, and outbound mail from the account to catch lateral phishing against colleagues and partners.

Give your SOC the speed to handle more threats with 20% less Tier-1 investigation time and 30% fewer escalations. Book an enterprise demo →

For CISOs and security leaders

SkyW4lker is a reminder that MFA is necessary but not sufficient. Three priorities:

  1. Close the device-code gap. Audit where device-code authentication is actually needed (typically headless devices, CLI tools, and some conferencing hardware). Block or tightly scope it with Entra Conditional Access everywhere else. This single control removes the attack’s payoff.
  2. Connect email, web, and identity telemetry. The kit only works because each stage is examined in isolation. Make sure the SOC can link a suspicious attachment, the phishing infrastructure it reaches, and the authentication event that follows.
  3. Shorten the investigation loop. Give Tier-1 analysts historical threat context and clear escalation criteria so routine phishing cases close at Tier 1, and reserve Tier 2 for incidents that truly need deeper work. Define a containment runbook for token-based compromise: revoke sessions, reset credentials, review app consents, and check for persistence.

  • 5200m[.]com, torvion[.]life, ghethim[.]com (hosts shared with Gabagool)
  • goldcreekconcrete[.]com, goldcreekconcrete[.]org (/skywalker/, /skyw4lker/ directories)
  • sdocshares.auth.outlook2026common.copilos26.csr-rooflng[.]com
  • pdocshared.payments2026.outlooks.common.ecmholdlnggroup[.]com
  • flow505.mooo[.]com, bigbrain.chickenkiller[.]com, off365acess.jumpingcrab[.]com

  • Sample lure SHA256: 9aa0b87974b9b4cd42603833b7ad44257578467d279b315a071108a5ed02c268
Conclusion

SkyW4lker is not a novel exploit; it is a well-engineered abuse of a feature Microsoft 365 ships by default.

Its growth from 20 to 200 sandbox submissions a month in a single quarter, its concentration on US enterprises, and its shared lineage with Gabagool all point to a phishing platform that will keep shipping new modes as long as device-code sign-ins stay open and SOCs keep treating phishing alerts one at a time.

The defensive answer is equally unglamorous: restrict device-code authentication where it is not needed, correlate email and identity events, and give analysts the ability to detonate what filters cannot inspect and to see, in one view, what the rest of the community has already found about the same infrastructure.

items.title: 6 Challenges SOC Leaders Should Turn into Priorities in 2027
items.summary: Security teams face mounting pressure to keep pace with increasingly complex threats while working within tight budgets and persistent staffing constraints. As attack techniques evolve and alert volumes rise, maintaining effective detection and investigation capabilities becomes increasingly demanding. In 2027, threat intelligence will play a growing role in helping SOC and MSSP teams recognize malicious activity earlier, investigate suspicious behavior faster, and make better use of analyst expertise. Achieving these gains requires intelligence to become part of everyday security workflows, informing decisions from initial detection through investigation and response. Six challenges mentioned in this article illustrate where organizations should focus their efforts in the year ahead. 1. Are You Detecting Threats Before They Become Incidents? One of the most effective ways to improve detection is to recognize malicious activity that has already been identified elsewhere. Without access to relevant intelligence, organizations may spend time investigating indicators that could have been flagged automatically. ANY.RUN’s internal analysis found that up to 30% of unique malicious IOCs identified during Interactive Sandbox investigations had already been observed and included in Threat Intelligence Feeds . This gives SOCs and MSSPs an opportunity to recognize known malicious activity earlier and reduce the time spent investigating previously identified threats. Turn intelligence from 16,000+ organizations into earlier detection to stay ahead of emerging threats. Integrate TI Feeds It’s also how security teams can improve detection without proportionally increasing investigative workloads. When an indicator appears in organizational telemetry, it can be matched against existing intelligence before an analyst begins a separate investigation. ANY.RUN TI Feeds bring this intelligence into SIEM, EDR, SOAR, and other security systems, helping organizations recognize known malicious activity earlier and use analyst time more strategically. Use TI Feeds to get access to live threat intelligence and detect current attacks By incorporating continuously updated intelligence into detection workflows, SOCs and MSSPs can identify threats sooner and reserve manual investigation for activity that requires deeper analysis. 2. Can Your SOC Prioritize Threats Without Spending Hours on Research? Alert volume is not the only challenge security teams face. The time required to understand which alerts represent genuine risk can be equally costly. A malicious IP address, suspicious domain, or file hash rarely provides enough information to determine its significance. Analysts need to understand its history, associated activity, and potential connection to broader campaigns. ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Lookup connects indicators with associated activity and previous analyses, while TI Reports provide insight into campaigns, infrastructure, techniques, and observed behavior. ANY.RUN TI Lookup provides deep threat context for faster investigations Enterprise users can take this investigation further with Related Threat Context , a brand-new capability connecting ANY.RUN Sandbox and TI Lookup . Analysts can move between behavioral analysis and related threat intelligence, uncovering links to previous investigations, indicators, and activity across their team and the wider threat intelligence ecosystem. Related Threat Context available to enterprise users in ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox This connection helps SOC and MSSP teams establish the significance of suspicious activity faster, identify relationships that might otherwise go unnoticed, and prioritize investigations based on stronger evidence. For security leaders, it supports more informed escalation decisions and better allocation of investigative resources. With threat context available across both analysis and intelligence workflows, analysts can spend less time researching individual indicators and more time addressing the threats that pose meaningful risk. 3. Are Investigation Bottlenecks Limiting Your SOC Capacity? When suspicious files or URLs require manual investigation, delays can accumulate across the entire security operation. The longer SOCs and MSSPs pend waiting for evidence or preparing environments, the fewer cases they can handle. ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox starts virtual machines in under 10 seconds, with Tier 1 reports typically available in around 40 seconds. Such reports also include AI-generated summaries and recommendations, giving analysts a quick overview of observed behavior and actionable next steps without having to review every detail first. Tier 1 reports with AI-generated summaries and recommendations in ANY.RUN’s sandbox These capabilities shorten the path from suspicious artifact to behavioral evidence, helping teams investigate more efficiently. For SOC and MSSP leaders, faster analysis translates into more than convenience. Shorter investigation cycles can increase case-handling capacity within existing staffing levels and help teams make decisions while relevant evidence is readily available. Analysts can also build on the related findings surfaced through Related Threat Context instead of repeating research into connected indicators or campaigns. This is particularly useful when investigating recurring threats or infrastructure across multiple customer environments. Reduce MTTR by 21 minutes and help your SOC resolve threats faster. Accelerate Your SOC Together, faster analysis and connected threat intelligence help security teams reduce investigation bottlenecks and make better use of the expertise they already have. 4. Is Your Threat Intelligence Producing Measurable Detection Value? Threat intelligence can become an expensive resource if it is collected but never translated into operational action. Indicators stored in separate platforms, manually transferred between systems, or reviewed only during investigations cannot consistently support proactive detection. ANY.RUN TI Feeds integrate validated malicious indicators into existing security infrastructure through APIs, SDKs, and STIX/TAXII-compatible workflows. Block the latest threats with fresh, noise-free TI Feeds This allows organizations to use intelligence across detection, enrichment, and response processes while building on their current security investments. For MSSPs, it can also support more consistent detection across customer environments. The business value comes from making intelligence operational: reducing manual transfer, extending the use of existing knowledge, and improving consistency in how threats are recognized. When intelligence reaches the systems responsible for monitoring and protecting the environment, it becomes a repeatable detection capability rather than another resource analysts must manage separately. 5. Can You Expand Detection Coverage Without Increasing Alert Fatigue? Increasing the number of detection rules or indicators can create the appearance of stronger security while simultaneously increasing the workload required to investigate alerts. The quality of intelligence matters as much as its quantity. ANY.RUN TI Feeds include 99% unique validated high-confidence IOCs, helping organizations incorporate intelligence that meets established quality criteria. For SOC leadership, this matters because every additional detection opportunity carries an operational cost. Reliable indicators can improve visibility without unnecessarily burdening analysts with low-value signals. A sustainable detection strategy therefore requires balancing coverage with confidence and the capacity to investigate resulting alerts. By prioritizing validated intelligence over sheer indicator volume, organizations can strengthen detection while keeping analyst workloads and alert fatigue under control. 6. Are You Getting More Value from Every Investigation? A security investigation should contribute more than a resolution to one incident. It can produce indicators, behavioral evidence, and intelligence that help identify similar threats in the future. When these findings remain isolated, organizations repeatedly spend resources investigating activity that could have been recognized earlier. By allowing existing investigations to inform subsequent detection and research, SOCs and MSSPs can avoid that issue. Relevant intelligence can also support recognition of similar threats across teams and customer environments. Detect up to 58% more threats and uncover malicious activity that might otherwise go unnoticed. Strengthen Your Defenses For decision makers, this creates an opportunity to improve operational efficiency over time: each investigation can strengthen future detection, reduce duplicated work, and increase the value of accumulated security knowledge. The SkyW4lker phishing kit investigation illustrates this in practice. By using Related Threat Context to connect suspicious URLs with previous Sandbox analyses, ANY.RUN analysts expanded the campaign cluster, uncovered additional phishing infrastructure, and identified technical links to the Gabagool kit. SkyW4lker detected in ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox For SOCs and MSSPs, this approach means a single suspicious URL can become a starting point for uncovering related campaigns and infrastructure across multiple investigations, helping teams reuse existing findings and accelerate threat hunting. When investigation findings feed back into detection, organizations can recognize recurring threats earlier and gradually reduce the effort required to investigate similar activity. Conclusion: Building More Efficient SOCs and MSSPs in 2027 The challenges facing security operations in 2027 are closely connected. Earlier detection reduces investigative demand, contextual intelligence improves prioritization, and faster analysis helps teams make decisions with less delay. Integrating validated intelligence into existing systems makes these improvements repeatable across the organization. Ultimately, SOC effectiveness in 2027 will be measured by how much security value organizations can generate from their existing resources: detecting threats earlier, accelerating investigations, and turning accumulated intelligence into lasting improvements in protection.

Threat intelligence can become an expensive resource if it is collected but never translated into operational action.

Indicators stored in separate platforms, manually transferred between systems, or reviewed only during investigations cannot consistently support proactive detection. 

ANY.RUN TI Feeds integrate validated malicious indicators into existing security infrastructure through APIs, SDKs, and STIX/TAXII-compatible workflows. 

Block the latest threats with fresh, noise-free TI Feeds 

This allows organizations to use intelligence across detection, enrichment, and response processes while building on their current security investments. For MSSPs, it can also support more consistent detection across customer environments. 

The business value comes from making intelligence operational: reducing manual transfer, extending the use of existing knowledge, and improving consistency in how threats are recognized. 

When intelligence reaches the systems responsible for monitoring and protecting the environment, it becomes a repeatable detection capability rather than another resource analysts must manage separately. 

5. Can You Expand Detection Coverage Without Increasing Alert Fatigue? 

Increasing the number of detection rules or indicators can create the appearance of stronger security while simultaneously increasing the workload required to investigate alerts. 

The quality of intelligence matters as much as its quantity. ANY.RUN TI Feeds include 99% unique validated high-confidence IOCs, helping organizations incorporate intelligence that meets established quality criteria. 

For SOC leadership, this matters because every additional detection opportunity carries an operational cost. Reliable indicators can improve visibility without unnecessarily burdening analysts with low-value signals. 

A sustainable detection strategy therefore requires balancing coverage with confidence and the capacity to investigate resulting alerts. 

By prioritizing validated intelligence over sheer indicator volume, organizations can strengthen detection while keeping analyst workloads and alert fatigue under control. 

6. Are You Getting More Value from Every Investigation? 

A security investigation should contribute more than a resolution to one incident. It can produce indicators, behavioral evidence, and intelligence that help identify similar threats in the future. 

When these findings remain isolated, organizations repeatedly spend resources investigating activity that could have been recognized earlier. 

By allowing existing investigations to inform subsequent detection and research, SOCs and MSSPs can avoid that issue. Relevant intelligence can also support recognition of similar threats across teams and customer environments. 

Detect up to 58% more threats and uncover malicious activity that might otherwise go unnoticed. Strengthen Your Defenses  

For decision makers, this creates an opportunity to improve operational efficiency over time: each investigation can strengthen future detection, reduce duplicated work, and increase the value of accumulated security knowledge. 

The SkyW4lker phishing kit investigation illustrates this in practice. By using Related Threat Context to connect suspicious URLs with previous Sandbox analyses, ANY.RUN analysts expanded the campaign cluster, uncovered additional phishing infrastructure, and identified technical links to the Gabagool kit.

For SOCs and MSSPs, this approach means a single suspicious URL can become a starting point for uncovering related campaigns and infrastructure across multiple investigations, helping teams reuse existing findings and accelerate threat hunting. 

When investigation findings feed back into detection, organizations can recognize recurring threats earlier and gradually reduce the effort required to investigate similar activity. 

Conclusion: Building More Efficient SOCs and MSSPs in 2027 

The challenges facing security operations in 2027 are closely connected. Earlier detection reduces investigative demand, contextual intelligence improves prioritization, and faster analysis helps teams make decisions with less delay.

Integrating validated intelligence into existing systems makes these improvements repeatable across the organization. 

Ultimately, SOC effectiveness in 2027 will be measured by how much security value organizations can generate from their existing resources: detecting threats earlier, accelerating investigations, and turning accumulated intelligence into lasting improvements in protection.

items.title: How to Export Exabeam Logs
items.summary: On the New-Scale Security Operations Platform, get an access token with your API key, then call the event search API with a filter, a time range and the fields you want. You get JSON back, one row per event. The Search app can also export results from the UI. Older on-premises Exabeam Data Lake deployments work differently; see the FAQ. Exabeam collects logs for behavior analytics and SIEM, and since its merger with LogRhythm it covers a big share of the market. Prime Core has 15,635 detection rules for Exabeam, mapped to 542 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key. Create a client ID and secret in the platform’s API key settings, with permission to search events. Your regional API host. It follows the pattern api. .exabeam.cloud, for example api.us-west.exabeam.cloud or api.us-east.exabeam.cloud. Query syntax. The event search uses Lucene-style filters, the same ones you type in the Search app. Test there first. Export with the Search API BASE="https://api.us-west.exabeam.cloud" # 1. access token TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/auth/v1/token" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"client_id\": \"$EXA_ID\", \"client_secret\": \"$EXA_SECRET\", \"grant_type\": \"client_credentials\"}" \ | jq -r '.access_token') # 2. event search curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/search/v2/events" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "filter": "host:\"web-03\"", "startTime": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "endTime": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z", "fields": ["*"], "limit": 10000 }' > exabeam_web03_1019.json jq -c '.rows[]' exabeam_web03_1019.json > exabeam_web03_1019.jsonl Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Token request fails Wrong client ID or secret, or the wrong regional host Check the key and region 403 on search The key lacks event search permission Grant search permission Empty results Filter syntax, or field names that differ Test the filter in the Search app Results stop at the limit limit reached Split the window FAQ I run Exabeam Data Lake on-premises. Does this apply? Not directly. The on-premises Data Lake is a different product with its own search and export options. What about LogRhythm? LogRhythm is part of Exabeam now, but LogRhythm SIEM keeps its own APIs.

items.title: mSecure tells users to change passwords but won’t say why
items.summary: Password manager mSecure has warned current and former customers to protect the confidential information stored in its app after detecting “suspicious activity.” But its advice about what users should do comes without an explanation of what happened or whose information might be at risk. The warning leaves users to decide whether to replace credentials—and whether it’s safe to store replacements in mSecure. While those are perfectly reasonable questions, mSecure’s warning does not answer them. In an email published by The Hacker News and sent to customers on November 3, mSecure’s developer, mSeven Software, said: “mSeven Software (‘mSeven’) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application. In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist.” The notice recommends that customers “immediately take steps to protect all confidential information” stored in mSecure. Those steps: “may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys.” But the notice does not identify the suspicious activity, when it occurred, which systems were involved, or whether anyone accessed customers’ stored information . The Register , which also reviewed the email, noted that the company had not explained whether customers’ secrets were exposed. How to be safe Because the scope of the incident is unknown, we recommend prioritizing your most important accounts while mSeven investigates. Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident. Users should not have to wait for a completed forensic investigation before receiving useful guidance. They need to know who should act, which credentials need attention, and whether the tool they would normally use to manage those changes remains safe to use. Until mSeven provides those answers, our advice is to prioritize your most important accounts, replace the relevant credentials through official services, and avoid destructive account resets: Change passwords through each service’s official website or app, beginning with your primary email, financial accounts, work accounts, and accounts used to recover access to other services. Use a new, different, strong password for each. Review two-factor authentication stored in the vault. If that could be compromised by unauthorized access, consider re-enrolling that account’s authenticator through the service’s security settings. For passkeys stored in mSecure, use each website or app’s account-security settings to remove the old registration and create a replacement with a different provider as a precaution. But make sure another working sign-in method is available first. Think carefully about where replacement credentials go. The notice does not establish whether saving new credentials in mSecure is safe. For users rotating important accounts now, using a different password manager temporarily is a reasonable precaution. We’ll keep you posted if we learn more about this incident, so stay tuned. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident.

items.title: Critical Ruby on Rails Flaw Could Let Hackers Steal Server Secrets Through Malicious Image Uploads
items.summary: A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails Active Storage lets an unauthenticated user upload a crafted image and make the server write files. If uploads use the Disk service, the same upload can make the server read files too. The Rails team rated the bug Critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and published the advisory on November 4, 2026. The flaw has no CVE ID yet. The flaw comes from how ImageMagick works. It picks a coder (a file format handler) based on what is inside a file, not on its name. Some coders act on other files named inside the image. Active Storage did not limit any of these coders, and its image analyzer runs as soon as a file is attached. So an attacker only needs to attach a crafted upload. No variant, preview, or analyze call is needed. Critical Ruby on Rails Flaw The files at risk usually include secret_key_base and credentials for outside systems. With those, an attacker may move on to remote code execution or reach other connected services. The Rails team also says one attack chain was reported , but they do not assume it is the only one. The researcher ryotak reported the bug through HackerOne. An app is affected only if all three of these are true. It uses ImageMagick through config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick , which is the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier. It runs ImageMagick under a policy that does not already block the coders involved, and the policies packaged by Debian and Ubuntu do not. And it accepts uploads from untrusted users. Affected versions are activestorage before 8.0.5.2, and 8.1 releases before 8.1.4.1. The fix ships an ImageMagick security policy. Rails adds its folder to MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH through MiniMagick.cli_env , so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick starts follows it. The policy blocks the MSL scripting coder, coders that read or delete other files, coders that fetch remote or local references, every Ghostscript-backed coder, and @filename indirection. The policy adds to the host’s rules instead of replacing them. This is not the first image-related Rails scare this year. Cyber Security News recently covered CVE-2026-66066 , a Rails Active Storage flaw that affected apps using libvips and could expose secrets such as secret_key_base and cloud keys. Researchers later saw that bug used in real attacks . Teams that patched in the summer should not assume they are safe now, because this is a different processor and a different fix. ImageMagick has also caused trouble outside Rails. A recent WordPress bug let Author-level users reach code execution because ImageMagick passed a disguised PostScript file to Ghostscript. A separate Discourse image pipeline exploit chained ImageMagick features to read server files. The lesson is the same each time: image tools do more than open pictures, so untrusted uploads need strict limits. First, upgrade activestorage to 8.0.5.2 or 8.1.4.1. Apps using :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or newer, and older versions fail with an error at boot. Apps that render PostScript or PDF through ImageMagick must allow the gs delegate again in the host’s policy.xml . Apps that replace MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clear the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix , or use their own MiniMagick::Shell do not get the shipped policy. They must copy its rules into ImageMagick’s system policy. GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies at all. Teams that cannot upgrade right away can copy the shipped rules into the system policy, for example /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml . At a minimum, they should block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate. Secrets need attention too. If attachments live on the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything in config/credentials.yml.enc , storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. The Rails team warns against keeping an exposed secret as a fallback. This fix is one of 21 security issues in the 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 releases . Others cover a Strong Parameters bypass, IP spoofing through the Forwarded header in 8.1, several cross-site scripting bugs in Action View, denial-of-service bugs, and session cookie problems. A second High-rated bug covers file read and code execution through Active Storage video previews and analysis. Security support for the 8.0 series ends on November 7, 2026, so teams on older lines should plan a move to 8.0 or later. Even with the patch, reviewing upload paths is worth the time. Teams should check logs for odd uploads and make sure no app runs with extra file permissions. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .
