Mi Scusi, My SCSI: Abusing iSCSI Target Server
items.summary: TL;DR – Enumerating the right connection strings lets you impersonate an iSCSI initiator and access whatever is stored on a shared virtual hard disk . Acknowledgments As always, I want to acknowledge the prior work done by peers: Himanshu Dwivedi – Who gave a talk at BlackHat back in 2005 (!!) on iSCSI Andrew Tierney – Who wrote a similar blog about abusing unauthenticated iSCSI Introduction In my last blog , I finally published about attacking Windows Server Failover Clusters (WSFC), and something from that work has been on my mind for the last few months. One requirement of the cluster setup process is to create shared storage that the member nodes use to replicate the cluster database. I glossed over this step in that blog, but that’s where I’ll be focusing for this one. The first time I set up a cluster, I followed this guide , which directs you to set up iSCSI storage. If you’re not familiar, iSCSI stands for Internet Small Computer System Interface ( RFC 7143 ). The iSCSI protocol evolved from SCSI. SCSI typically connects devices and transfers data between them and their hard disk drives over a bus network . iSCSI was designed to allow this communication to occur over TCP. This is really bringing back some of the CompTIA A+ studying I did back in the day. The key thing to know about iSCSI storage is that it operates at a layer below file storage (files in directories) and uses block-level storage (think hard drives) instead. The iSCSI target server service is part of the File and Storage Services server roles, and installation is straightforward from the Add Roles and Features menu in Server Manager. However, configuring the service requires a few steps. First, select a physical drive to use as the iSCSI virtual disk, name it, and choose the virtual drive size. The very next step is to set up a unique name for the iSCSI Target. The target name is part of the iSCSI Name Structure, which consists of a type designator and a unique name string. Microsoft uses the iSCSI Qualified Name (IQN) type of iSCSI Name and concatenates the host server’s hostname with the chosen string. The IQN looks like this when constructed: iqn.1991-05.com.microsoft:hyv-dc01- iscsi-target-name Next, set up the access servers, which are the clients that will connect to and use the virtual disk. This requires identifying an “initiator” (more on this later). There are four options to choose from to identify the initiator: IP, DNS, MAC, or IQN, and IQN is the recommended method of identification and the type we’ll be taking advantage of later. To obtain the initiator IQNs from the client servers, start the iSCSI initiator service from the Tools menu in Server Manager. In the Configuration tab of the iSCSI initiator menu, the initiator’s IQN is built automatically. The final step is to optionally configure CHAP authentication for initiator connections. Since the guide says not to, we’ll skip this step. If everything went smoothly, the chosen initiator servers should have a new disk attached. No Authentication? You’ve probably already guessed where this is going. We’ve created a valid session between the client and server where authentication is optional. Section 6.3 explains how the “Login Phase” establishes a connection and session between an initiator and target server: “The initial Login Request of any connection MUST include the InitiatorName key=value pair. The initial Login Request of the first connection of a session MAY also include the SessionType key=value pair. For any connection within a session whose type is not “Discovery”, the first Login Request MUST also include the TargetName key=value pair.” “The Login Phase MAY include a SecurityNegotiation stage and a LoginOperationalNegotiation stage or both, but MUST include at least one of them. The included stage MAY be empty except for the mandatory names.” Without CHAP authentication configured, all that’s required to “login” is to know what host has the iSCSI target service installed along with its iSCSI target IQN and its client initiator IQNs. Finding where the target service is installed is the easiest part. If the server is joined to Active Directory, when the iSCSI target service first starts, it registers an SPN on the host computer’s AD account. Run a simple LDAP query, and we’ve got a list of iSCSI target servers. The hint for answering how to get the iSCSI target’s IQN was in the text from the RFC above: “…For any connection within a session whose type is not “Discovery”…”. There are two types of sessions for iSCSI: a normal operational session, as we’ve already discussed, and a Discovery session. “Discovery-session – a session only opened for target discovery. The target MUST ONLY accept text requests with the SendTargets key and a Logout Request with the reason “close the session”.” The SendTargets key refers to the SendTargets operation that was designed as a feature to reduce friction when configuring the service. The way it works is that when the session is established using the “Discovery” session type, an iSCSI target name IQN does not need to be specified; only the initiator IQN. On top of that, if presented with an authorized IQN (using that term loosely here; it’s just whatever is in the access server list) and the “All” command, the server must respond with a list of all of the IQNs the initiator has access to. Now all that’s left is to discover the iSCSI initiator IQNs. Fortunately, these are predictable. You probably noticed in the iSCSI initiator properties screenshot above that the IQN of the initiator is constructed using the dNSHostName of the host server. iqn.1991-05.com.microsoft: hyv-node1.ludus.domain In my experience, there’s no rate limiting or brute-force protection on the service. That means we could query AD, or even DNS, for the DNS names of every domain-joined computer to build a list of potential initiator IQNs, then attempt a Discovery session with each one until the server responds with its IQN. I mentioned before that the key thing to know is we’re targeting block-level storage. This means we can enumerate the right values to impersonate an iSCSI initiator and access whatever is stored on the virtual hard disk while completely avoiding any NTFS permissions. It’s important to note that if BitLocker or a similar solution was used to encrypt the drive, this obviously becomes invalid. Demo Attack Path Let’s go through what I’d consider the worst-case scenario end-to-end. To start, we’ve already located an iSCSI target server through SPN enumeration in AD. We’ve also built a list of potential initiator IQNs through dNSHostName attribute enumeration. With those in hand, use scuzzy.py to iterate over the list and recover the iSCSI target IQN. Next, check if authentication is required with the login command. If login succeeds, there’s no CHAP required, and you’re free to pilfer. Enumerate what’s available on the drive with the ls command. There are a few directories available, including the testvm directory. Interestingly, you can also view the $RECYCLE.BIN directory, which leaks the SIDs of users who have had interactive logons on hosts that mounted the volume. Navigating to that path shows the drive stores Hyper-V VMs, including their virtual hard disks and snapshots. Now, download the .VHDX file. With the VHDX downloaded, use a tool like SkelSec’s adiskreader to mount the disk and navigate the file system of the virtual machine (VM). From here, it’s as simple as extracting the SAM , SYSTEM , and SECURITY registry hives from the C:\Windows\System32\config directory . Oh, and wouldn’t you know it? It’s a domain controller (DC) too, so grab the NTDS.dit file from C:\Windows\NTDS as well. Finally, dump credential material from the recovered files with Impacket’s secretsdump.py. Obviously, not every drive will contain DC hard disks, so I mixed my own Googling with some LLM-powered research and found the most common uses were clustered resources like Hyper-V, MSSQL, Exchange DAGs, etc., followed by third-party backup solutions. The next question is how common these configurations are. items.summary_html:
TL;DR –  Enumerating the right connection strings lets you impersonate an iSCSI initiator and access whatever is stored on a shared virtual hard disk.

Acknowledgments

As always, I want to acknowledge the prior work done by peers: 

Himanshu Dwivedi – Who gave a talk at BlackHat back in 2005 (!!) on iSCSI

Andrew Tierney – Who wrote a similar blog about abusing unauthenticated iSCSI

Introduction

In my last blog, I finally published about attacking Windows Server Failover Clusters (WSFC), and something from that work has been on my mind for the last few months. One requirement of the cluster setup process is to create shared storage that the member nodes use to replicate the cluster database. I glossed over this step in that blog, but that’s where I’ll be focusing for this one.

The first time I set up a cluster, I followed this guide, which directs you to set up iSCSI storage. If you’re not familiar, iSCSI stands for Internet Small Computer System Interface (RFC 7143). 

The iSCSI protocol evolved from SCSI. SCSI typically connects devices and transfers data between them and their hard disk drives over a bus network. iSCSI was designed to allow this communication to occur over TCP. This is really bringing back some of the CompTIA A+ studying I did back in the day. The key thing to know about iSCSI storage is that it operates at a layer below file storage (files in directories) and uses block-level storage (think hard drives) instead. 

The iSCSI target server service is part of the File and Storage Services server roles, and installation is straightforward from the Add Roles and Features menu in Server Manager. 

However, configuring the service requires a few steps. First, select a physical drive to use as the iSCSI virtual disk, name it, and choose the virtual drive size. The very next step is to set up a unique name for the iSCSI Target. 

The target name is part of the iSCSI Name Structure, which consists of a type designator and a unique name string. Microsoft uses the iSCSI Qualified Name (IQN) type of iSCSI Name and concatenates the host server’s hostname with the chosen string. The IQN looks like this when constructed:

iqn.1991-05.com.microsoft:hyv-dc01-iscsi-target-name

Next, set up the access servers, which are the clients that will connect to and use the virtual disk. This requires identifying an “initiator” (more on this later). There are four options to choose from to identify the initiator: IP, DNS, MAC, or IQN, and IQN is the recommended method of identification and the type we’ll be taking advantage of later.

To obtain the initiator IQNs from the client servers, start the iSCSI initiator service from the Tools menu in Server Manager. In the Configuration tab of the iSCSI initiator menu, the initiator’s IQN is built automatically.

The final step is to optionally configure CHAP authentication for initiator connections. Since the guide says not to, we’ll skip this step. If everything went smoothly, the chosen initiator servers should have a new disk attached.

No Authentication?

You’ve probably already guessed where this is going. We’ve created a valid session between the client and server where authentication is optional. 

Section 6.3 explains how the “Login Phase” establishes a connection and session between an initiator and target server:

“The initial Login Request of any connection MUST include the InitiatorName key=value pair. The initial Login Request of the first connection of a session MAY also include the SessionType key=value pair.  For any connection within a session whose type is not “Discovery”, the first Login Request MUST also include the TargetName key=value pair.”

“The Login Phase MAY include a SecurityNegotiation stage and a LoginOperationalNegotiation stage or both, but MUST include at least one of them. The included stage MAY be empty except for the mandatory names.”

Without CHAP authentication configured, all that’s required to “login” is to know what host has the iSCSI target service installed along with its iSCSI target IQN and its client initiator IQNs. Finding where the target service is installed is the easiest part.

If the server is joined to Active Directory, when the iSCSI target service first starts, it registers an SPN on the host computer’s AD account. Run a simple LDAP query, and we’ve got a list of iSCSI target servers.

The hint for answering how to get the iSCSI target’s IQN was in the text from the RFC above: “…For any connection within a session whose type is not “Discovery”…”. There are two types of sessions for iSCSI: a normal operational session, as we’ve already discussed, and a Discovery session.

“Discovery-session – a session only opened for target discovery.  The target MUST ONLY accept text requests with the SendTargets key and a Logout Request with the reason “close the session”.”

The SendTargets key refers to the SendTargets operation that was designed as a feature to reduce friction when configuring the service. The way it works is that when the session is established using the “Discovery” session type, an iSCSI target name IQN does not need to be specified; only the initiator IQN. On top of that, if presented with an authorized IQN (using that term loosely here; it’s just whatever is in the access server list) and the “All” command, the server must respond with a list of all of the IQNs the initiator has access to.

Now all that’s left is to discover the iSCSI initiator IQNs. Fortunately, these are predictable. You probably noticed in the iSCSI initiator properties screenshot above that the IQN of the initiator is constructed using the dNSHostName of the host server. 

iqn.1991-05.com.microsoft:hyv-node1.ludus.domain

In my experience, there’s no rate limiting or brute-force protection on the service. That means we could query AD, or even DNS, for the DNS names of every domain-joined computer to build a list of potential initiator IQNs, then attempt a Discovery session with each one until the server responds with its IQN.

I mentioned before that the key thing to know is we’re targeting block-level storage. This means we can enumerate the right values to impersonate an iSCSI initiator and access whatever is stored on the virtual hard disk while completely avoiding any NTFS permissions. It’s important to note that if BitLocker or a similar solution was used to encrypt the drive, this obviously becomes invalid.

Demo Attack Path

Let’s go through what I’d consider the worst-case scenario end-to-end. To start, we’ve already located an iSCSI target server through SPN enumeration in AD. We’ve also built a list of potential initiator IQNs through dNSHostName attribute enumeration. With those in hand, use scuzzy.py to iterate over the list and recover the iSCSI target IQN.

Next, check if authentication is required with the login command. If login succeeds, there’s no CHAP required, and you’re free to pilfer.

Enumerate what’s available on the drive with the ls command. There are a few directories available, including the testvm directory. Interestingly, you can also view the $RECYCLE.BIN directory, which leaks the SIDs of users who have had interactive logons on hosts that mounted the volume.

Navigating to that path shows the drive stores Hyper-V VMs, including their virtual hard disks and snapshots.

Now, download the .VHDX file. 

With the VHDX downloaded, use a tool like SkelSec’s adiskreader to mount the disk and navigate the file system of the virtual machine (VM).

From here, it’s as simple as extracting the SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY registry hives from the C:\Windows\System32\config directory. Oh, and wouldn’t you know it? It’s a domain controller (DC) too, so grab the NTDS.dit file from C:\Windows\NTDS as well.

Finally, dump credential material from the recovered files with Impacket’s secretsdump.py.

Obviously, not every drive will contain DC hard disks, so I mixed my own Googling with some LLM-powered research and found the most common uses were clustered resources like Hyper-V, MSSQL, Exchange DAGs, etc., followed by third-party backup solutions. The next question is how common these configurations are. We queried our BloodHound Enterprise (BHE) customer tenants and found about 50% had at least one computer with the SPN, with the maximum number being close to 700.

Defensive Recommendations
  1. Enable CHAP authentication for Windows iSCSI
  2. IPSEC is available to mitigate any sort of network sniffing 
  3. Arguably the most effective thing you can do is have proper network segmentation and host-based firewall configurations to isolate the drive
Final Thoughts

I haven’t tested this in production myself, so absolutely test and verify there will not be any outages or downtime caused by abusing this. I also still haven’t answered why the iSCSI target role registers an SPN when I’ve only seen CHAP get used as the authentication protocol. I can say I spent some time reversing it along with Codex, and it looks like it was intended to be used for DCOM? I could be wrong and, maybe, you can figure out the answer.

The post Mi Scusi, My SCSI: Abusing iSCSI Target Server appeared first on SpecterOps.

items.title: How to Export Securonix Logs
items.summary: Generate an API token, run your Spotter query through the Securonix REST API (/ws/spotter/index/search), and save the events as JSON. When the source sent raw text, the original line is usually kept in the raw event field. Spotter in the UI can export results too. Securonix pulls in large volumes of activity data for UEBA and SIEM, which makes it a rich place to export an investigation slice from. Prime Core has 14,283 detection rules for Securonix, mapped to 620 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start API access. You need a Securonix user that’s allowed to use the API. Tokens are generated with that user’s credentials and have a validity period you choose. Your tenant URL. Cloud tenants usually look like https:// .securonix.net/Snypr. Retention. Hot data is searchable directly in Spotter. Older data may sit in long-term storage that needs extra steps to search. Export with the REST API BASE="https:// .securonix.net/Snypr" # 1. token, valid for one day TOKEN=$(curl -sS -H "username: $SNX_USER" -H "password: $SNX_PASS" -H "validity: 1" \ "$BASE/ws/token/generate") # 2. Spotter query for a time window curl -sS -G -H "token: $TOKEN" "$BASE/ws/spotter/index/search" \ --data-urlencode 'query=index=activity AND devicehostname="web-03"' \ --data-urlencode 'eventtime_from=10/19/2026 00:00:00' \ --data-urlencode 'eventtime_to=10/20/2026 00:00:00' \ > snx_web03_1019.json # 3. one event per line jq -c '.events[]' snx_web03_1019.json > snx_web03_1019.jsonl Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Token request fails Wrong credentials, or the user can’t use the API Check the user’s API permission Empty results Query syntax, or the date format doesn’t match Test the query in Spotter; check the format Only part of the results Paging not followed Request the following pages with the query ID Old events missing Data has moved out of hot storage Check long-term storage options FAQ Can I export violations and threats instead? Those are detections and have their own API calls. For LogTotal, export the activity events behind them. Is Securonix on-premises different? The API is broadly the same; the base URL is your own server. Check your version’s API guide.

items.title: Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Lets Hackers Hijack Software Updates and Execute Code as Root
items.summary: A newly disclosed bug in APT, the package manager behind Debian and Ubuntu, can let a network spy swap a trusted software package for a bad one. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-109518 and can end in code running with root rights, the highest level of control on a Linux system. Debian announced the issue on November 4, 2026, and credited researcher Max Justicz with finding it. APT checks each package against signed data before it installs anything. This flaw lets an attacker get around that check. According to Debian, APT can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives it the same address. When APT resumes an interrupted download, it handles the file incorrectly, opening a short window to replace the package after it has been verified. The package that gets installed is then the attacker’s version, not the checked one. The attacker must sit between the computer and the archive server. That could be someone on the same network, a rogue proxy, or a malicious mirror. The flaw also depends on hard link reuse, and it needs the client to follow redirects and retry a download. These conditions make the attack harder than a simple remote hit, but public Wi-Fi, hijacked routers, and compromised mirrors make them realistic. Debian APT Flaw Lets Hackers Hijack Updates The bug only works when APT’s retry setting, Acquire::Retries , is above zero. That value is 3 by default on Debian 12 (bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, so older releases are not affected in their default setup. The Debian Security Tracker lists these states: Bookworm: version 2.6.1 is vulnerable and 2.6.2 is fixed. Trixie: version 3.0.3 is vulnerable and 3.0.4 is fixed. Testing and unstable (forky, sid): version 3.3.5 is vulnerable. The tracker points to advisory DSA-6607-1 for trixie and DLA-4880-1 for bookworm. Ubuntu and other derivatives need their own patches, so users should watch their vendor’s notices. The Debian advisory for trixie says the problem is fixed in APT 3.0.4 and urges users to upgrade. The same update also closes several out-of-bounds access bugs. For the upstream project, APT 3.3.6 changes the download methods to open target files exclusively. This stops two downloads from touching the same file. The release also rejects DEB packages that lack the required Version field and fixes a sorting bug in the dependency solver. APT has had a similar scare before. In 2019, Justicz found a remote code execution bug in apt, tracked as CVE-2019-3462. It also let a man-in-the-middle run code as root through a redirect. His workaround then was to turn off redirects with -o Acquire::http::AllowRedirect=false . The new flaw is a different bug, but the lesson is the same. Redirects and download handling are risky parts of any update tool. Run apt update and apt upgrade on trusted networks, and confirm the installed APT version matches the fixed one for your release. Avoid untrusted mirrors and proxies until you have patched. Prefer HTTPS mirrors where you can, because they make interception harder. As a stopgap on unpatched systems, setting Acquire::Retries to 0 removes one required condition, though it can make updates less reliable on poor connections. Update tools run with full trust, so one bad package can hand over a whole server. Our earlier coverage of Linux supply chain security essentials explains why checking package integrity matters. Readers who run Debian can also see how large patch batches land in our report on Debian’s 1,313-flaw kernel update . No public reports of active use have surfaced so far. Patching now is still the safest move. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Cloud Agent, now in a Container: Host Security for Nodes You Can’t Touch
items.summary: A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are. Key Takeaways The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub , bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager. It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet , so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install. A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM . Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate. Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane. The AI Era Is a Container Era The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now. That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it. Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads. The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways. Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container. Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically. The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload. The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account . It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager. Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher. The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it. Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64 ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane. Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster. Why It Matters: The Benefits Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection. Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place. Qualys has been building this coverage across the major cloud platforms for years: Securing Red Hat CoreOS on OpenShift Scanning AWS Bottlerocket in Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS Scanning Container-Optimized OS in Google Kubernetes Engine Qualys for Microsoft Azure Linux in AKS and Azure Container Instances Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. It also runs on the RPM- and Debian-based distributions that make up the bulk of self-managed and cloud Kubernetes nodes today. That’s a meaningful change. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring. Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember. Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model. One Image Across Every Operating System You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them. Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool. Full-Stack Coverage at a Glance The Containerized Cloud Agent runs the complete Qualys Cloud Agent on every node, assessing the host OS against the Qualys KnowledgeBase for vulnerabilities and against Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks through Qualys Policy Audit. items.summary_html:
A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are.

Key Takeaways
  • The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub, bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager.
  • It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install.
  • A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM.
  • Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate.
  • Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane.
The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

  1. Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.
  2. Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

  • Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64
  • ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm
How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane.

Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster.

Why It Matters: The Benefits

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. If you can’t install anything, you can’t install a traditional agent, and many teams have run these nodes blind. The Containerized Cloud Agent closes that gap. It runs as a privileged container with the host mounts it needs to assess the underlying OS, so Bottlerocket, COS, and CoreOS nodes get the same vulnerability and compliance visibility as a conventional Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) server, with no changes to the host image and no compromise to the immutability that made you choose that OS in the first place.

Qualys has been building this coverage across the major cloud platforms for years:

  • Securing Red Hat CoreOS on OpenShift
  • Scanning AWS Bottlerocket in Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS
  • Scanning Container-Optimized OS in Google Kubernetes Engine
  • Qualys for Microsoft Azure Linux in AKS and Azure Container Instances
Your Choice of Agent on Mutable Linux, Too

The Containerized Cloud Agent isn’t limited to immutable operating systems. It also runs on the RPM- and Debian-based distributions that make up the bulk of self-managed and cloud Kubernetes nodes today. That’s a meaningful change. Previously, a RHEL or Ubuntu node meant installing the RPM or DEB package, full stop. Now you choose. Teams with a mix of virtual machines (VMs) and containers can keep the package on VMs and use the Containerized Cloud Agent on cluster nodes. Teams that are all-in on Kubernetes can standardize on the Containerized Cloud Agent everywhere and never manage a host package again. Either way, the data lands in the same place, with the same detections and the same TruRisk scoring.

Deployment That Fits How You Already Run Kubernetes

The Containerized Cloud Agent is a DaemonSet, which means the orchestrator guarantees one agent per node, on every node, for the life of the cluster. Autoscaling node pools, spot instances that get reclaimed, and cluster upgrades that replace every node are all handled without a ticket, a script, or a human. Coverage becomes a property of the cluster rather than a task someone has to remember.

Because it’s delivered as a Helm chart and YAML manifests, the agent lives in the same GitOps repository as your workloads. Upgrading is a tag change and a pull request. Rolling back is a revert. Node selectors and tolerations let you target specific pools, and the same manifest works across dev, staging, and production. Security stops being the exception to your deployment model.

One Image Across Every Operating System

You don’t need a Bottlerocket build, a CoreOS build, and an Ubuntu build. A single Containerized Cloud Agent image runs across all supported operating systems. That collapses your deployment matrix: one image to vet through your supply-chain controls, one image to pin and version, one DaemonSet manifest to maintain. When a new agent release ships, it’s one tag to update across the entire estate. Images that comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) are available for environments that require them.

Complete Coverage Across Intel and ARM

Cluster node pools increasingly mix x86 and ARM instances, with Graviton, Cobalt, and Axion sitting alongside traditional Intel and AMD nodes. Images are published for both Intel/x64 and ARM, so a multi-architecture cluster gets consistent coverage without special-casing by pool.

Full-Stack Coverage at a Glance

The Containerized Cloud Agent runs the complete Qualys Cloud Agent on every node, assessing the host OS against the Qualys KnowledgeBase for vulnerabilities and against Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks through Qualys Policy Audit. Here’s how coverage splits across the stack:

CapabilityCovered byVulnerability ManagementHost: Containerized Cloud Agent. Containers: TotalCloud KCSDrift detectionTotalCloud KCSCompliance (CIS Benchmarks)Data plane: Qualys Policy Audit. Control plane: TotalCloud KCS (Kubernetes Security Posture Management, or KSPM)Threat detection and response/runtime securityTotalCloud KCS, via eBPF runtime sensors

Findings from both Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit flow into the same Enterprise TruRisk Platform views, dashboards, and workflows your teams already use. A Kubernetes node is just another asset with a Qualys TruRisk score, sitting next to the VM, the laptop, and the cloud account, and prioritized the same way.

Getting Started

  2. Download the deployment YAMLs or use the Qualys Helm chart.
  3. Deploy as a DaemonSet to your cluster with your Agent Activation Key, following the Intel or ARM getting started guide.

Platform-specific guides are available for AWS Bottlerocket, Google COS, and Red Hat CoreOS.

The Common Container tiles will appear in the Download and Install Cloud Agent workflow, with your activation key, supported OS list, and installation steps right there.

items.summary: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities.
items.summary_html:
Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​  Introduction

Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website.

Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. 

About the vulnerabilities: 
  1. CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption
  2. CVE-2026-109619- RCE via stale global state  

Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. 

The vulnerabilities relate to PHP handling of memory when a request terminates abnormally, for example due to memory exhaustion or a fatal error. Under certain conditions, improper memory handling could allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution. 

Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. 

Refer to vendor guidancefor patching of different versions of PHP.

Recommended action: upgrade PHP 

We recommend that customers: 

  1. Upgrade all PHP deployments to a patched version, including virtual machines, containers, base images, and platform runtimes. We suggest prioritizing internet-facing workloads. 
  2. Rebuild and redeploy container images that include their own PHP runtime, since updating the host does not update PHP inside an image. 
  3. Migrate to a supported PHP branch if the branch currently in use no longer receives security fixes. 
  4. Treat the Azure WAF mitigations below as a temporary, supplementary measure. They address a specific technique and do not remediate the underlying vulnerabilities. 
Azure WAF protection

If you are unable to upgrade PHP to a patched version immediately, apply the following mitigations in the interim -

  • Azure Front Door WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the managed rule for response-side mitigation.
  • Application Gateway WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the rewrite rule for response-side mitigation.
  • Application Gateway for Container WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation.

See below sections for details.

Mitigation using custom rules

These custom rules can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities. Depending on application traffic, the rules may result in false positives and affect legitimate requests. They are intended as temporary mitigations and do not replace the need to upgrade PHP.  Learn more: Azure WAF custom rules for PHP2Shell mitigation. 

Request-side signals alone may not be sufficient to reliably identify certain exploitation attempts. Signals in the server response can provide additional evidence that malicious activity has occurred, enabling more targeted mitigation with higher confidence and lower false positives.  For this vulnerability, Azure WAF identifies known malicious patterns in the session and removes the potentially malicious elements from the response before it reaches the client. This provides an additional layer of protection for supported exploitation scenarios, while patching PHP remains necessary to fully address the underlying vulnerability.  

Azure Front Door WAF: managed rule 

A managed rule to handle potential attack vector in response is available for Azure Front Door WAF, its details are as follows: 

  • Rule group: MS-ThreatIntel-Response-CVEs 
  • Rule ID: 99006001 
  • Default state: disabled. Customers need to enable the rule. 

Supported rulesets: DRS 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2. Unlike other WAF rules, this rule does not block or challenge any traffic. When the rule identifies malicious signals in the session that provides strong evidence of exploitation, it removes the potentially malicious elements from the response while leaving the remainder of the response unchanged. Mitigation for this rule takes effect only when the rule action is set to Block on anamoly. Please note that the response side mitigation does not generate WAF log entries or hit counts.   

Application Gateway WAF: rewrite rule

Customers can apply an interim mitigation now using the HTTP header rewrite capability of Application Gateway, which is available on v2 SKUs. A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway is expected to roll out at a later date. Until then, we recommend the following rewrite rule: 

       1. Create a rewrite rule in a rewrite set associated with your routing rule(s). 

       2. Add a condition that evaluates the Set-Cookie response header against the following regular expression: 

^PHPSESSID=(?:[a-zA-Z0-9\-]|%2[Cc])*(?:[^a-zA-Z0-9\-;%]|%(?!2[Cc]))+[a-zA-Z0-9\-]*[^;]+; 

  

          3. Set the action to delete the matching Set-Cookie response header. Alternatively, the header can be set to a replacement value of your choice.                     Please note that setting a value overwrites the entire header, including attributes such as Path=/;. 

 

 Additional considerations: 

  • The rule applies only to a Set-Cookie header that matches the pattern. Other Set-Cookie headers in the same response are not affected. 
  • We recommend validating the rule on a non-production gateway before broader deployment. 

For further information, see Rewrite HTTP headers and URL with Azure Application Gateway. 

Application Gateway for Containers (AGC): A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway for Containers is expected to roll out at a later date. In the interim, customers can apply the custom rules. Application Gateway for Containers does not support regex-based rewrite rules on HTTP response. Restrict request size 

The proof-of-concept payloads analyzed so far are about 60 MB each. Attackers may be able to craft smaller payloads, so treat size limits as an extra layer of protection, not a mitigation on their own. Whatever rule set version you use, we recommend the following: 

Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers 

The proof-of-concept payloads are well above the default maximum request body size of 128 KB on Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Containers. We recommend setting the maximum request body size in your WAF policy to the smallest value your application needs. Learn more.  

Azure WAF on Azure Front Door 

To limit request body size, create a custom rule with a size constraint. For request body checks, the size is measured on the decoded body. Set the limit to the smallest value your application needs and make sure request body inspection is enabled in your WAF policy settings. 

The following example blocks request bodies larger than 40 KB. This rule supports limits of up to 128 KB. 

 

{ "name": "BlockLargeRequestBody", "priority": 130, "enabledState": "Enabled", "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariable": "RequestBody", "operator": "GreaterThan", "negateCondition": false, "matchValue": [ "40960" ] } ] } Conclusion 

Following PHP security guidance and upgrading to a patched version is the recommended and complete remediation. Azure WAF mitigations can help reduce exposure during the upgrade period, and we encourage customers to upgrades at the earliest opportunity. 

Changelog
  • 10/26/2026 9:00 AM PST - Updated with additional guidance around request size restrictions
  • 10/21/2026 7:00 PM PST – Updated with additional guidance around custom rules

items.title: Exploiting PHP Foundational Vulnerabilities
items.summary: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely used open-source server-side scripting language designed for web development. It has over the years gained widespread acceptance for its ease of use and programming/scripting abilities and is notably the scripting language that implements the popular WordPress application. WordPress is the most popular content management system (CMS) in the world powering approximately 42% of worldwide websites, and nearly 60% of websites that use a CMS. On October 21 st , 2026, the PHP project reported the following two CVEs and released a patch for the vulnerabilities. These CVEs are related in that they both involve memory use from the heap in PHP worker processes. CVE-2026-109618: Remote Code Execution via Out of Memory Condition (OOM) When PHP experiences a memory exhaustion condition known as “out-of-memory (OOM)”, it uses the standard C function longjmp() to transfer execution into another function for a fatal error and exit. During multipart parsing of an HTTP request, if the OOM condition is triggered while the request state is partially initialized, the fatal exit and shutdown reads invalid memory, which can lead to remote code execution (RCE). Susceptibility to this vulnerability is implementation dependent. The highly popular Apache “mod_php” for example unconditionally executes the longjmp() in an OOM condition making it vulnerable. CVE-2026-109619: Remote Code Execution via Stale Global Memory Pointer State PHP worker processes retain a global state memory pointer to any freed request memory. It is possible that the global state is not properly reset in some scenarios or even that memory is repopulated after a reset. Fatal errors such as the above OOM condition will skip the pointer reset. This effectively translates into memory use-after-free condition and remote code execution becomes possible. Background Exploitability of these CVEs is non-trivial with some pre-conditions to be met and multiple possibilities/avenues of potential attack. In this blog, we will focus purely on CVE-2026-109618 to see if we can get a single HTTP POST exploitation vector. We must first have an application configuration and components that allows for the upload of multipart form data. Within PHP, there was a feature released in version 5.4.0 that introduced a configuration switch called “session.upload_progress”. In the implementation, the switch defaults to being enabled. Below is a snippet from the PHP manual: This feature processes multipart form data in a function called php_session_rfc1867_callback() in the PHP session handling API. All the HTTP POST request data in the session API is processed before any application code runs. The callback handler function: Creates temporary session state files with attacker controllable data. Runs on any PHP web application that accepts HTTP POST requests. No authentication is required during the session API handling of these requests. Therefore, this callback function in the PHP code is an excellent candidate to allow a threat actor to trigger an out-of-memory condition and potentially gain remote code execution. Lab Setup To explore these vulnerabilities, we need a reliable lab setup. A docker container is the easiest way to get up and running with Apache mod_php. As you might imagine, Docker Hub publishes a number of images for the community already. Having said that, I learned through the process of banging my head against a brick wall repeatedly that the PHP project to their credit had recompiled PHP with the fixes and back ported into older versions of the docker containers. Bravo, but it was unexpected and frustrating for me while getting the lab up and running! The following setup information formed the basis of my lab: Libphp.so was compiled fresh directly from the php-8.4.26 source code with all of the same configuration switches that are commonly used in an Apache mod_php environment. The following PHP initialization/configuration directives were placed in /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/custom.ini to create a stable controlled environment. The most important statements are making sure that the upload progress switch is enabled, and that the max memory size for HTTP posts is a little more constrained to help us trigger an out of memory condition sooner during upload. I created a basic index.php and placed it in the /var/www/html root directory. All it did was print some version info and the value the upload_progress.enabled flag. I disabled Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) in the docker host. More on this later. I used a local AI model to speed up the debugging and researching process. Specifically, I used Qwen3.8-27b running on an Nvidia RTX-4090 GPU. After finishing the vulnerable docker container setup using the reference image of php:8.4.26-apache, I used docker commit to save a vulnerable image as vuln_php. I had the AI model write a simple Python script called oom_probe.py to successively send larger and larger multipart form data HTTP POST requests until I observed an out of memory response from the PHP server. I was then able to see stale session files lying around in /tmp/sessions as expected. Initial Attack Path (Low Hanging Fruit) There is another defect that allows for a reasonably easy initial attack path and that is the multipart form handler code in PHP that accepts the session cookie from the form data without checking the session.use_only_cookies setting. This gives us session fixation, which means that we will know the session identifier, and will directly map to the stale session file we leave on the server. Notably the “name” parameter sent in the post request is stored directly in the temporary session state file. The session state file that is written when the OOM condition is triggered will not be deleted leaving the attacked supplied data in the “name” parameter within the file contents. Below is an example using my probing script of injecting data into this field and then looking at the file on the target docker container. All we need from there is some form of local file inclusion in the PHP of the application and we get command injection ability by writing PHP code into the filename variable we post. For example, we could write the following text into the filename field that remains on disk in the stale session state files: Then if any other PHP script includes this state file, we have an execution of the command. However, this path depends on a local file inclusion vulnerability in the application. I dropped a simple vulnerable PHP script onto the web server with a direct file inclusion to verify this. Higher Complexity Attack Path An interesting observation is that the multipart form upload code in the session handling API will potentially trigger the out of memory condition before any application code runs. More specifically, the Zend engine ( zend_bailout() function in zend.c of the php source code) will be executed when the Zend HashTable structure is only partially initialized. The last line of code in zend_bailout() is the LONGJMP() macro that ultimately just executes a longjmp() to transfer program execution control into the shutdown and exit function for this request. Since all this code is written in C, any time we are about to shut down a process, developers are obligated to cleanup memory. This is commonly referred to as a destructor function, and in the C language, context must be manually implemented. Without getting too far in the weeds, the bottom line is that the Zend HashTable structure, when initialized for an HTTP request, contains memory pointers for object destruction functions. If we can somehow influence the value of one of these memory pointers, we will be able to control execution. From a high level, these are the parts and sequence of the exploit: OOM triggered by large multipart form data HTTP POST to index.php . Form data contains a payload designed to pad out a forged Zend object beyond the max memory limit of the PHP process. The zend_bailout() function is called, which triggers the process shutdown functions that are dealing with only a partially initialized HashTable. The forged object type of 8 in payload sends execution control to the zend_objects_store_del() function. zend_objects_store_del() calls the destructor function handler (a memory pointer). This object handler is from our forged object we created in payload and sends execution to a new jump target address we call POP4. POP4 sets the RDI register to the command string we want to execute and pops the other registers off the stack. POP4 then calls libc system() to execute an O/S command. What POP4 represents here is a return-oriented programming (ROP) gadget we are using as a springboard to get the right things put into the right registers before our system call. The astute reader is going to recognize that to make all this work, we need some static memory addresses. This is the point in the blog where I tell you that I did all this work in a docker container after switching Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) off, and hard coded the memory addresses of both LIBC, and the loaded LIBPHP object. ASLR is a great defense mechanism; however, during the course of an exploit POC development there are already complexities of understanding the exact nature of the vulnerability, in this case the memory layout of the heap, and we need to break the development steps down into manageable steps minimizing complexity at each step. Once we have achieved success with a defensive mechanism like ASLR disabled, we can move forward with further development with defenses re-enabled steadily growing the exploit capability. ASLR Enabled Attack Path It is possible to adapt this attack path for different vulnerable versions of PHP and for a normal implementation where ASLR is not disabled. In the case where ASLR is not disabled, we would probably modify the attack to leverage the zip_system() function, which is an implementation of the system() function inside of libphp. This optionally eliminates the additional base address requirement of libc, but is not absolutely required. We need a method to leak address information about libphp.so when attempting to adapt for a non-ASLR attack path. This is where the second CVE-2026-109619 becomes useful. In my reading and research, along with some additional AI model assistance, I discovered that we could get a vulnerable PHP server to leak memory address information using the Set-Cookie header over HTTP. This memory address disclosure is an over-HTTP arbitrary read made possible by stale PS(id) / PS(send_cookie) state being consumed by the upload-progress session path before RINIT. It prints attacker-directed heap/libphp memory into the PHPSESSID cookie. To achieve success with the ASLR enabled attack path, we need to be able to pin the attack to a single PHP worker process. The reason for this is that the attack will occur in stages. The initial stage will be used to leak memory addresses in the cookie headers of the response, and then the attack stage to push the exploit into the heap. Because ASLR is enabled, we need both stages of the attack to leverage the same PHP worker process. Otherwise said, the library base memory addresses will stay consistent in the same worker process. How can we possibly know the Apache/PHP configuration on the target server? The answer to this question is . . . that we just don’t know. Thus, in the final proof of concept attack script, we introduce a parameter called —workers , which sets the target worker process count to an arbitrary number. During the attack, we use some Python threads to keep the workers – 1 count of processes busy. This is so we can create the condition whereby our attack itself will attack only one worker for all stages. In the final developed exploit, I decided to keep using the system() function from libc. Therefore, we have to leak the base memory address for libc as well as libphp. Here is the execution sequence flow as documented by the AI model: And finally, what you have been waiting for, here is a screenshot of the exploit actually running with the injected command string as follows: You will of course notice that we wrote the output to a file. This is because the output from the worker process is not reflected back in the HTTP response. We used a simple PHP script to fetch the contents, which reads as follows: I am pretty sure you can use your imagination on how to take this further. Anyway, without delaying the anticipation any longer, here is the screenshot output of a running exploit against an Apache/PHP server using 10 worker processes in its configuration. Thoughts on AI Assistance When developing these attack paths using the assistance of an AI model, I leveraged OpenCode as the agentic harness, a full copy of the php-8.4.26 source code, a recompiled copy of libphp.so from this source that was vulnerable as well as some example exploitation code from “CookieEngineer” that followed a similar path. You might be thinking that I prompted the AI model once saying something like “go find a vulnerability based on this CVE,” but you would be incorrect. To get good and expedient results from the local AI model, I examined the vulnerability carefully, read lots of source code, and got very specific with a lot of my prompting. In other words, I leveraged the AI model as my intern to accelerate development paths while the real directed thinking and additional knowledge was coming from myself and my research. More to the point, I stepped the AI model through this in small discrete steps for better quality results, and for my own personal understanding. PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely used open-source server-side scripting language designed for web development. It has over the years gained widespread acceptance for its ease of use and programming/scripting abilities and is notably the scripting language that implements the popular WordPress application. WordPress is the most popular content management system (CMS) in the world powering approximately 42% of worldwide websites, and nearly 60% of websites that use a CMS.

On October 21st, 2026, the PHP project reported the following two CVEs and released a patch for the vulnerabilities. These CVEs are related in that they both involve memory use from the heap in PHP worker processes.

  • CVE-2026-109618: Remote Code Execution via Out of Memory Condition (OOM)

    When PHP experiences a memory exhaustion condition known as “out-of-memory (OOM)”, it uses the standard C function longjmp() to transfer execution into another function for a fatal error and exit. During multipart parsing of an HTTP request, if the OOM condition is triggered while the request state is partially initialized, the fatal exit and shutdown reads invalid memory, which can lead to remote code execution (RCE).

    Susceptibility to this vulnerability is implementation dependent. The highly popular Apache “mod_php” for example unconditionally executes the longjmp() in an OOM condition making it vulnerable.

  • CVE-2026-109619: Remote Code Execution via Stale Global Memory Pointer State

    PHP worker processes retain a global state memory pointer to any freed request memory. It is possible that the global state is not properly reset in some scenarios or even that memory is repopulated after a reset. Fatal errors such as the above OOM condition will skip the pointer reset. This effectively translates into memory use-after-free condition and remote code execution becomes possible.
Background

Exploitability of these CVEs is non-trivial with some pre-conditions to be met and multiple possibilities/avenues of potential attack. In this blog, we will focus purely on CVE-2026-109618 to see if we can get a single HTTP POST exploitation vector.

We must first have an application configuration and components that allows for the upload of multipart form data. Within PHP, there was a feature released in version 5.4.0 that introduced a configuration switch called “session.upload_progress”. In the implementation, the switch defaults to being enabled. Below is a snippet from the PHP manual:

This feature processes multipart form data in a function called php_session_rfc1867_callback() in the PHP session handling API. All the HTTP POST request data in the session API is processed before any application code runs. The callback handler function:

  • Creates temporary session state files with attacker controllable data.
  • Runs on any PHP web application that accepts HTTP POST requests.
  • No authentication is required during the session API handling of these requests.

Therefore, this callback function in the PHP code is an excellent candidate to allow a threat actor to trigger an out-of-memory condition and potentially gain remote code execution.

  • Libphp.so was compiled fresh directly from the php-8.4.26 source code with all of the same configuration switches that are commonly used in an Apache mod_php environment. 
  • The following PHP initialization/configuration directives were placed in /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/custom.ini to create a stable controlled environment. The most important statements are making sure that the upload progress switch is enabled, and that the max memory size for HTTP posts is a little more constrained to help us trigger an out of memory condition sooner during upload.
  • I created a basic index.php and placed it in the /var/www/html root directory. All it did was print some version info and the value the upload_progress.enabled flag.
  • I disabled Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) in the docker host. More on this later.
  • I used a local AI model to speed up the debugging and researching process. Specifically, I used Qwen3.8-27b running on an Nvidia RTX-4090 GPU.
  • After finishing the vulnerable docker container setup using the reference image of php:8.4.26-apache, I used docker commit to save a vulnerable image as vuln_php.
  • I had the AI model write a simple Python script called oom_probe.py to successively send larger and larger multipart form data HTTP POST requests until I observed an out of memory response from the PHP server.

items.title: How to Export ArcSight Logs
items.summary: How you export from ArcSight depends on which part of it holds the data. For history, search in ArcSight Logger and export the results. For a repeatable route, forward events from Logger or a SmartConnector to a syslog collector as CEF, and export the collector’s file. One thing decides how useful any export is: the original raw event is kept only if your SmartConnectors were configured to preserve it. OpenText ArcSight has been running in large SOCs for a long time, which means it often holds years of history nobody else has. Prime Core has 21,311 detection rules for ArcSight, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Which ArcSight? Logger stores and searches events. ESM correlates them. Recon is the newer search and analytics layer. For bulk export, Logger is usually the right place. Is the raw event there? SmartConnectors normalize events into CEF fields. They keep the original text only with raw event preservation turned on. If it was off, you can export the normalized CEF events, but not the original lines. Rights and retention. You need a Logger user that can search the storage groups involved, and the data has to still be within Logger’s retention. Option 1: Logger search and export In Logger, open Search , set the time range, and write the query using CEF field names, for example destinationHostName = “web-03” AND deviceVendor = “Unix”. Run it and check the count. Export the results. Option 2: Forward CEF to a syslog collector Set up a small Linux collector with rsyslog listening on UDP or TCP 514. Then point a Logger forwarder or a SmartConnector destination at it, in CEF over syslog. Logger forwarders can also send a past time range as a one-off. Then cut the window you need from the collector’s file: grep 'web-03' /var/log/arcsight/cef.log > arcsight_web03.log Each line is a CEF record: a header with vendor, product and event name, then key=value extensions. If raw event preservation was on, the original text sits in the rawEvent field. Option 3: Logger REST API Logger also has a REST API for logging in and running searches, which suits scripted exports. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. Review. What this looks like on real data. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix No original log text in the export Raw event preservation was off on the SmartConnector Export normalized CEF; turn preservation on for the future Search finds nothing Wrong storage group, or outside retention Check storage groups and retention Collector receives nothing Firewall, wrong port or protocol Check each hop; tcpdump -n port 514 on the collector Long CEF lines cut off UDP message size limits Use TCP syslog FAQ Can I export from ESM instead? ESM active channels can export, but ESM holds correlated and filtered data. For complete history, Logger is the better source. Is CEF good enough without the raw event? For many detections, yes: CEF keeps the key fields. You lose fields the connector didn’t map, and the exact original wording.

How you export from ArcSight depends on which part of it holds the data. For history, search in ArcSight Logger and export the results. For a repeatable route, forward events from Logger or a SmartConnector to a syslog collector as CEF, and export the collector’s file. One thing decides how useful any export is: the original raw event is kept only if your SmartConnectors were configured to preserve it.

OpenText ArcSight has been running in large SOCs for a long time, which means it often holds years of history nobody else has. Prime Core has 21,311 detection rules for ArcSight, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Which ArcSight? Logger stores and searches events. ESM correlates them. Recon is the newer search and analytics layer. For bulk export, Logger is usually the right place.

Is the raw event there? SmartConnectors normalize events into CEF fields. They keep the original text only with raw event preservation turned on. If it was off, you can export the normalized CEF events, but not the original lines.

Rights and retention. You need a Logger user that can search the storage groups involved, and the data has to still be within Logger’s retention.

Option 1: Logger search and export
  1. In Logger, open Search, set the time range, and write the query using CEF field names, for example destinationHostName = “web-03” AND deviceVendor = “Unix”.
  2. Run it and check the count.
  3. Export the results. 
Option 2: Forward CEF to a syslog collector

Set up a small Linux collector with rsyslog listening on UDP or TCP 514. Then point a Logger forwarder or a SmartConnector destination at it, in CEF over syslog. Logger forwarders can also send a past time range as a one-off. Then cut the window you need from the collector’s file:

grep 'web-03' /var/log/arcsight/cef.log > arcsight_web03.log

Each line is a CEF record: a header with vendor, product and event name, then key=value extensions. If raw event preservation was on, the original text sits in the rawEvent field.

Option 3: Logger REST API

Logger also has a REST API for logging in and running searches, which suits scripted exports.

Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.
  2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review. 

What this looks like on real data.

When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixNo original log text in the exportRaw event preservation was off on the SmartConnectorExport normalized CEF; turn preservation on for the futureSearch finds nothingWrong storage group, or outside retentionCheck storage groups and retentionCollector receives nothingFirewall, wrong port or protocolCheck each hop; tcpdump -n port 514 on the collectorLong CEF lines cut offUDP message size limitsUse TCP syslog
FAQ

Can I export from ESM instead?

ESM active channels can export, but ESM holds correlated and filtered data. For complete history, Logger is the better source.

Is CEF good enough without the raw event?

For many detections, yes: CEF keeps the key fields. You lose fields the connector didn’t map, and the exact original wording.
