items.title: Scammers Use Microsoft Azure to Host Fake Windows Security Alerts Seen at 80 Organizations
items.summary: Scammers are abusing Microsoft Azure to host fake Windows security alerts that pressure users into calling fraudulent support numbers. Between March and October 2026, the same fake Microsoft support kit reached users at 80 organizations. New landing pages were still appearing daily as of November 2, showing that the operation remained active. These figures describe exposure to scam pages, not 80 confirmed network breaches. The attack begins with an advertisement on a legitimate website. Clicking it sends the visitor to an Azure-hosted page displaying alarming security messages and a fake support chat. Similar Azure tech support scams have used Bing advertisements to reach business users, demonstrating how paid placements can turn routine browsing into a dangerous encounter. Researchers from PIXM identified the scam kit and traced part of its supporting infrastructure in a November 2 investigation. Scammers Use Microsoft Azure Their analysis describes a browser-based support scam rather than a confirmed malware infection. The Azure landing pages imitate “System Error” and “Windows Firewall” warnings, with every element directing visitors toward a toll-free number. Behind the warning screen, JavaScript requests a telephone number from a central service using JSONP, a technique that loads a response through a script. An advertising-manager parameter tells the service which operator’s number to return. This lets the organizers change numbers across deployed pages without rebuilding each site. The code also includes a fallback number if the request fails. A tracking pixel records the displayed number, campaign, publisher website, and advertising exchange. These details help operators connect incoming calls to particular advertising campaigns. A page captured on April 3, 2026. The bar at top center reads “…web.core.windows[.]net – 若要退出全屏模式，请按 esc”, Chrome’s “To exit full screen, press Esc” in Chinese (Source – PIXM) The setup resembles legitimate pay-per-call marketing, but the calls originate from deceptive security warnings. The manager list expanded from three names in May to four in July, suggesting multiple participants rather than one person maintaining every page. The broader technique echoes separate fake Microsoft security alerts campaigns that use disposable cloud-hosted pages to funnel visitors toward scam call centers. However, PIXM’s attribution has an important limit: the specific back end it investigated accounted for exposure at 11 organizations. Other operations used the same fake page across the wider group of 80 organizations. Infrastructure Clues, Business Risks, and Defenses Several clues suggest Mandarin-speaking developers and connections to mainland China. Script comments and error messages used Simplified Chinese, while one page family displayed a copied Chinese full-screen notice. The telephone service exposed a default BaoTa server-panel page in Chinese. Registration records also listed a Hubei address, although PIXM stressed that self-reported registration information alone cannot establish attribution. Tracking data identified placements associated with Whitepages, Legacy.com, Us Weekly, MSN, KMBC, WordHippo, Juno webmail, and the health section of US News & World Report. PIXM said these publishers were not complicit. The advertisements passed through programmatic exchanges, and reviewers did not necessarily see the same destination presented to targeted visitors. The immediate danger is the conversation that follows the warning. Scammers commonly persuade callers to install remote-access software, charge for unnecessary repairs, or introduce refund and bank-impersonation schemes. Separate Microsoft Teams impersonation attacks show how legitimate remote-management software can also become an access channel when users accept instructions from an impersonator. That comparison does not establish malware deployment in this campaign. Defenders should block the listed malicious infrastructure through DNS controls or secure web gateways and restrict remote-access software to approved support workflows. Employees should close suspicious tabs or force-quit the browser rather than call displayed numbers. Blocking the telephone service disrupts dynamic number delivery, but the fallback means this should not be treated as complete protection. Trusted cloud hosting does not make a rendered warning trustworthy. items.title: EU AI Act transparency rules show why businesses can’t afford to wait
items.summary: By Khush Kashyap, Senior Director of Governance, Risk and Compliance at Vanta Transparency goes hand in hand with AI. Or at least it’s meant to. Until now, transparency has mostly depended on how forthcoming people are about using AI. Detection tools can’t carry that weight on their own. That is now changing. The EU AI Act’s transparency requirements , which came into effect this August, call on providers and deployers of certain AI systems to label or disclose content that is generated or manipulated by AI. Now, providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started to act. This reflects a broader shift in AI regulation: transparency and traceability are moving from principles to practical requirements. But, for businesses, the picture is far from clear. First, as regulators attempt to establish workable standards for identifying AI-generated content, the technology itself continues to evolve, making it a moving target. Second, while parts of the EU AI Act’s regulatory framework are moving forward, others, such as high-risk AI obligations are being pushed back. This leaves businesses with a clear choice: wait for every detail to be settled, or start building the visibility and accountability that meaningful transparency requires. Watermarking is only the tip of the AI governance iceberg Watermarking is seen by many to reflect the EU AI Act requirements. But businesses must consider the limitations of the technology and whether it can provide reliable, lasting proof that content was generated or manipulated by AI. A text watermark doesn’t survive much. Paraphrase it, translate it, or run it through a model that doesn’t watermark, and it’s gone. OpenAI’s own approach to EU text provenance rules makes the point with numbers: replacing a quarter of the words with synonyms dropped detection from roughly 92% to 17%, and shorter passages are far harder to detect in the first place. The debate around watermarking tells us a lot about the practical challenges of regulating AI. This approach may help demonstrate transparency, but it cannot explain how AI is being used, whether human oversight took place or who is accountable for the outcome. Look at how differently two providers have answered the same rule: Anthropic watermarks everywhere, while OpenAI turns it on by default only in the EU. If the technical layer is this unsettled, your governance can’t depend on it. For this, broader AI governance is what’s needed. The wider context of the EU AI Act These implications extend far beyond watermarking.The Digital Omnibus, a separate amending regulation finalised in July, has pushed the high-risk deadlines out — to December 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2028 for AI in regulated products — and has also changed some of the Act’s definitions. For instance, the definition of a “safety component” has been narrowed, so systems used purely for user assistance, performance optimisation, automation or convenience no longer automatically qualify — though the carve-out falls away the moment a failure could endanger health or safety. These changes may affect which systems fall into the highest-risk categories, but requirements and prohibitions demonstrate that the regulatory direction of travel remains towards greater accountability, transparency and evidence. My advice is simple: don’t set your pace by regulatory deadlines. If you wait for every standard to be finalised before you act, you end up doing it all in a rush — and that’s how you get security theatre, where more time goes into proving security than improving it. The combination of new transparency requirements and extended timelines gives businesses two things they rarely have: clarity about the direction of travel, and more time. They should therefore treat it as a rare opportunity to build meaningful governance infrastructure before they are forced to do so. Three priorities organisations should tackle now Action doesn’t always equal governance. If organisations focus on producing labels or paperwork without understanding how AI is being used in practice, they are still exposing themselves to the same risks. They may understand whether their organisation uses AI, but not where it appears across products, workflows and customer interactions. The following priorities can help businesses build the foundations they will need as future obligations take effect. Build a complete AI asset inventory Everything starts with visibility. Begin by identifying every AI system across your organisation, including tools introduced informally by teams or embedded within existing products and across your network. Then understand what each system does, the data it processes, who owns it and its likely risk classification under the EU AI Act. This can help you understand where controls and evidence are still missing, and where risk is likely to grow. Conduct AI impact assessments For higher-risk AI systems, establish documented evaluations before deployment and when your systems change. Assess factors such as bias, human oversight, transparency, accountability, security and data handling in a structured way. These assessments can serve a similar practical purpose to GDPR’s DPIAs by recording the risks identified, the controls applied and the decisions made. The Act has its own fundamental rights impact assessments for certain deployers, but those sit in the delayed high-risk package — another reason to build the muscle now. Create clear AI governance structures Develop practical AI policies that cover acceptable use, data handling, human review and third-party AI tools. As part of this, assign clear ownership for AI governance across your organisation’s security, privacy, legal, compliance and product teams. Be sure to maintain audit trails that show how systems were approved, what controls were applied and how risks are monitored over time. Governance should be proportionate to risk and scale as regulation evolves. This is how it supports responsible innovation, instead of slowing it down. Turning transparency into action Whatever side you take, the watermarking debate tells us that AI regulation is becoming increasingly tangible. But we must avoid interpreting delays in the EU AI Act as reduced regulatory ambition or a free pass from responsibility. Instead, it must be treated as additional preparation time. Organisations that spend this time building robust AI governance programmes that give them the confidence to understand how AI works, the evidence to show how it is governed and the means to build better, more trusted products. Right now, we are focused on whether AI-generated content can be identified. Instead, we need to ask ourselves if we can explain where AI is being used, what risks it creates and what controls are in place to manage it. So that transparency goes beyond the checkbox and becomes an ongoing capability.

items.title: Critical SolarWinds Dameware Flaw Could Allow Attackers to Compromise Remote Systems
items.summary: SolarWinds has warned about a critical command injection flaw in its Dameware remote support software. It is tracked as CVE-2026-28336 and carries a severity score of 9.9 out of 10. The bug could let an attacker take over a computer that an IT team is controlling remotely. Dameware is widely used by help desks and administrators to connect to and fix remote computers. Since the tool runs with strong access, a flaw in it is risky for any company that depends on it. SolarWinds published the advisory on November 3, 2026, and urged users to update quickly. Analysts at SolarWinds noted the problem in their security advisory. No malware is tied to this flaw, and the advisory does not report any attacks in the wild. It says the issue could lead to the compromise of the remotely controlled host. This is not the first Dameware bug to draw attention, since an earlier Dameware privilege escalation flaw was fixed in 2025. Critical SolarWinds Dameware Flaw Could Allow Attackers Command injection happens when software accepts input from a user and passes it to the system without checking it properly. An attacker can then slip in their own commands. In this case, the attacker must already be logged in, so the flaw needs valid access first. The CVSS vector (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) shows the flaw can be used over a network with low complexity. It needs only low privileges and no user interaction. It also changes scope, which means the impact can spread beyond the weak component to the remote machine. Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all rated high. The issue affects SolarWinds Dameware 2026.3 and all earlier versions. The fixed release is Dameware 2026.3.1. Greg Bernatowicz of the Boeing Enterprise Security Red Team received credit for finding it, according to the official SolarWinds advisory . Why SolarWinds Users Should Act Fast Attackers like remote support tools because one stolen login can open many systems. Recent history shows how quickly SolarWinds bugs get abused. Hackers were seen exploiting Web Help Desk flaws to install extra remote access tools. SolarWinds has been patching many products this year. Recent updates covered critical SolarWinds Observability flaws that allowed remote code execution. The company also released Serv-U security fixes for 15 vulnerabilities in July. Administrators should upgrade Dameware to 2026.3.1 now, review who holds Dameware accounts, and remove any that are not needed. They should also limit network access to the tool and watch logs for strange commands. items.title: French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack Amid Reports of $133 Million Theft
items.summary: French banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed a cyberattack that enabled fraudulent transactions, following reports linking the institution to cryptocurrency theft exceeding $133 million. The bank says the incident is contained, operations are gradually resuming, and customer assets remain unaffected. It has not confirmed the reported loss figure. The group notified regulatory and supervisory authorities after detecting the attack. Teams temporarily suspended certain transactions to prevent further fraud while checking systems and adding security measures. According to its statement, customers experienced delays involving some transfers, but their funds remain protected. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT linked Arkéa to suspicious cryptocurrency withdrawals after initially describing the victim as an unnamed European institution. His first findings identified more than $106 million withdrawn on November 1. An additional $27 million later pushed his estimate above $133 million. These figures remain investigative estimates, not losses verified by the bank. The case draws attention to fraudulent payments moving through financial channels. Cybersecurity News previously covered BREEZE COMET’s attacks on financial firms , which involved trusted access and unauthorized transfers. However, no evidence currently connects that group or its methods to the Arkéa incident. items.title: CVE-2026-119977: WordPress Core RCE Flaw Exploited During Software Upgrades
items.summary: A high-severity vulnerability in WordPress Core is being actively targeted in attacks, prompting the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, the vulnerability carries a CVSS score of 8.1 and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server during a WordPress Core upgrade. The vulnerability stems from a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition in the WordPress upgrade process. During full-package Core updates, WordPress temporarily stages installation files in predictable, web-accessible locations. Attackers can repeatedly probe these locations and attempt to reach installer components during the brief period in which an upgrade is taking place. WordPress addressed the issue in version 7.1.4, released on October 28, 2026. The vulnerability affects WordPress versions 4.7 through 7.1.3, while security fixes have also been backported to eligible older branches. WordPress stresses that only the latest release is actively supported. The risk has moved beyond theoretical exploitation. Wordfence telemetry cited by The Hacker News recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged setup-config.php installer paths during the first 21 hours after disclosure. CISA subsequently confirmed evidence of exploitation and required applicable U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate the vulnerability by November 6, 2026. Security teams can use the SOC Prime Platform to strengthen detection coverage against emerging exploitation techniques and hunt for suspicious activity associated with vulnerable internet-facing systems. Detect CVE-2026-119977 exploitation by monitoring abnormal requests to WordPress upgrade locations, unexpected PHP execution, newly created administrative accounts, suspicious files, and post-exploitation behavior. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. Contact Sales CVE-2026-119977 analysis CVE-2026-119977 is classified as a TOCTOU race condition under CWE-367 and has a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. Its vector reflects network-based exploitation requiring no privileges or user interaction, with high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Attack complexity is rated high because successful exploitation depends on reaching a vulnerable resource during a narrow upgrade window. CVE-2026-119977 affects WordPress Core releases from version 4.7 through 7.1.3. The weakness is not tied to a third-party plugin or theme; it exists in the Core software upgrade mechanism itself. The issue occurs during full-package Core upgrades. WordPress temporarily extracts the new package into a staging location beneath the wp-content/upgrade directory before replacing the existing installation. In affected releases, portions of this staging location can be predictable and reachable from the web while the update is underway. One particularly important component is the staged setup-config.php installer. An unauthenticated attacker who correctly predicts the temporary path and reaches that component before WordPress completes cleanup may be able to interact with the staged installation and ultimately execute PHP code on the server. This creates an unusual exploitation model. A vulnerable WordPress site is not necessarily continuously exploitable. Instead, the attacker must catch the site during the brief period in which a full-package upgrade exposes the staging files. Researchers indicate that the opportunity may last only seconds. Attackers can compensate for that limitation through automation. Rather than making a single request, threat actors can continuously poll potential upgrade paths and wait for a target to begin updating. Wordfence observed attackers repeatedly requesting variations of staged installer locations, demonstrating that real-world actors quickly understood how to target the race condition. The large volume of observed requests should nevertheless be interpreted carefully. The reported figures represent blocked requests or exploitation attempts and do not mean that every request resulted in successful remote code execution. Exploitation still requires the request to coincide with an active full-package upgrade and other required server conditions. Wordfence’s initial telemetry showed more than 18,500 requests against staged installer paths in the first 21 hours. GBHackers subsequently reported nearly 59,000 attempts blocked within a 24-hour period, while The Hacker News cited additional telemetry demonstrating continued exploitation activity. Independent honeypot telemetry cited by The Hacker News recorded exploitation attempts on October 30, further supporting CISA’s decision to classify the vulnerability as actively exploited. CISA’s addition of the flaw to KEV significantly raises the urgency for organizations operating public WordPress infrastructure. At the time of writing, the reviewed sources do not document a broadly available, publicly validated CVE-2026-119977 PoC repository. However, public exploit code is not required to establish risk because exploitation attempts have already been observed at scale and CISA has confirmed active exploitation. WordPress 7.1.4 changes the vulnerable upgrade process. According to the available technical reporting, the remediation includes making staging locations less predictable, introducing additional protections against direct access, and preventing staged configuration data from being promoted in an unsafe manner. WordPress credited security researcher Umut Bayram with reporting the upgrade-process weakness. Version 7.1.4 was released on October 28, 2026, and the CVE record was subsequently published on October 31. For CVE-2026-119977 detection, defenders should pay particular attention to web requests targeting unusual paths beneath wp-content/upgrade, especially requests referencing staged copies of setup-config.php. Repeated requests across multiple possible staging directories may indicate automated probing attempting to win the race condition. Successful exploitation can potentially provide remote PHP code execution in the context of the affected web server. Defenders should therefore correlate suspicious upgrade-path requests with subsequent evidence such as unexpected PHP files, modification of WordPress configuration data, unfamiliar administrator accounts, malicious plugins, unusual child processes spawned by the web server, or unexpected outbound connections. Public reporting has not identified a comprehensive set of attacker-specific CVE-2026-119977 IOCs such as stable command-and-control domains or malware hashes. This makes behavior-based detection particularly important. Requests to predictable staging paths, suspicious activity during an update window, and post-exploitation modifications provide more durable hunting opportunities than relying exclusively on static indicators. CVE-2026-119977 Mitigation The primary CVE-2026-119977 mitigation is to update WordPress immediately. WordPress 7.1.4 contains the security fix, and fixes have also been made available or backported for eligible older release branches. Organizations should prioritize migration to the latest actively supported WordPress version rather than relying indefinitely on legacy security backports. Administrators should take the following actions: Upgrade internet-facing WordPress installations to version 7.1.4 or later. Verify that automatic updates completed successfully rather than assuming that an update was applied. Inventory older WordPress installations, including forgotten development, staging, and legacy sites. Review web server and WAF logs for requests targeting wp-content/upgrade and staged setup-config.php paths. Investigate unexpected PHP files, new WordPress administrator accounts, unauthorized plugins, and unexplained configuration changes. Review outbound connections and web-server child processes for evidence of post-exploitation activity. Ensure WAF protections operate early enough in the request path to cover direct requests to temporary PHP files. Consider restricting direct web access to temporary upgrade directories where operationally feasible. Web application firewall rules can reduce exposure to automated exploitation attempts, but they should not be treated as a replacement for patching. Because the vulnerable resource can exist temporarily outside the normal WordPress request flow, administrators should verify that their WAF deployment actually inspects direct requests to staged PHP files. Organizations that upgraded while active exploitation was already underway should also consider retrospective investigation. Completing the update removes the vulnerable behavior but does not prove that the server was not compromised while the vulnerable staging directory was available. Review access logs surrounding the precise upgrade timestamp. Requests to the affected staging paths occurring immediately before or during the upgrade should receive additional scrutiny. Security teams should then correlate those requests with file-system changes, WordPress account modifications, PHP execution, suspicious network connections, and other post-exploitation indicators. If compromise is suspected, isolate the affected host where practical, preserve relevant web, application, authentication, and system logs, and collect suspicious files before remediation. Credentials and secrets accessible to the WordPress/PHP process should be considered potentially exposed and rotated based on the findings of the investigation. CISA’s inclusion of the vulnerability in KEV confirms that remediation should be treated as an immediate operational priority rather than a routine patch-cycle item. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies were directed to address the issue by November 6, 2026. FAQ What is CVE-2026-119977 and how does it work? CVE-2026-119977 is a high-severity unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in WordPress Core caused by a TOCTOU race condition in the upgrade process. During full-package Core updates, WordPress temporarily stages installation files in predictable web-accessible locations. An attacker who reaches the staged installer during this brief window may be able to execute arbitrary PHP code on the server. When was CVE-2026-119977 first discovered? WordPress credited security researcher Umut Bayram with reporting the vulnerability. WordPress released version 7.1.4 containing the fix on October 28, 2026, while the CVE record was published on October 31. The reviewed sources do not specify the exact date on which the vulnerability was originally reported privately to WordPress. What is the impact of CVE-2026-119977 on systems? Successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on the affected WordPress server during the vulnerable upgrade window. Depending on the privileges of the web server process and the attacker’s follow-on actions, this could lead to website compromise, malicious file deployment, data theft, persistence, credential exposure, or further intrusion into connected infrastructure. Can CVE-2026-119977 still affect me in 2026? Yes. WordPress installations running affected versions remain at risk, and exploitation is occurring in the wild. CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after evidence of active attacks, while security vendors have recorded tens of thousands of requests attempting to reach vulnerable staging paths. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-119977? Upgrade WordPress to version 7.1.4 or a later supported release immediately and confirm that the update completed successfully. Review web server and WAF logs for requests targeting temporary upgrade directories, inspect sites for unauthorized PHP files, administrator accounts, plugins, or configuration changes, and investigate systems that were updated while exploitation attempts were underway. Organizations should also monitor WordPress and CISA advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-119977 as the exploitation landscape develops.

items.title: From Crisis to Control: Cybersecurity Meets High Performance
items.summary: In motorsports and cybersecurity, every second counts: we discussed this on October 20th, 2026, together with cybersecurity decision-makers from the DACH region at the Red Bull Ring in Spielberg. Alexander Luig from Ontinue presented on the use of AI agents in the SOC. Marc Nimmerrichter then used examples from Certitude’s own vulnerability research to explain how much AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and why valuable time is lost in many cyber incidents due to a lack of preparation. Sarah Ellensohn from Ontinue moderated the panel discussion “Keeping Your AI Agents Under Control: Best Practices for Managing AI Agents Securely” featuring decision-makers from various large corporations. It became clear that while AI agents are becoming new colleagues, critical decisions are still made by humans. After a shared lunch, the Driving Experience was next on the agenda. Our guests took to the track in cars with 330 PS (about 325 hp) under the hood. Patrick Friesacher, a former Austrian Formula 1 driver, explained the cars and what to look out for while driving. Speed matters in motorsports just as it does in cybersecurity, but the race is usually decided during the preparation phase: Those who clarify responsibilities, decision-making processes, and permissions before a cyberattack have to improvise less and therefore lose less time. Thank you to all our guests for joining us and to our partner Ontinue for the excellent collaboration. You can find a few impressions in the photo gallery below: Further Reading To learn more about the risks posed by AI agents and what organizations can do now, read our research article The New Reality in Cybersecurity: AI Agents, Acceleration, and Asymmetry.

items.title: Critical Barracuda Security Flaws Could Let Hackers Bypass Authentication and Gain Root Access
items.summary: Barracuda has disclosed two security vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to affected appliances when exploited together. The flaws affect several Barracuda security products, but exploitation requires access to a device’s administrative interface, making exposed management systems a key concern for defenders. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, were disclosed on November 2, 2026. Barracuda has released patches and urged customers to install the latest firmware and verify that security updates have reached their devices. Its advisory does not report active exploitation or identify an associated attack campaign. Barracuda researchers identified the vulnerabilities, not a malware strain. The distinction matters because the disclosure describes weaknesses in appliance access controls and command handling rather than a documented malware infection. According to the official Barracuda security advisory, combining these weaknesses could give an attacker root access to an affected device. Critical Barracuda Security Flaws CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorization bypass affecting Barracuda Email Security Gateway, commonly called ESG. It carries a CVSS score of 9.3. CVE-2026-111560 is a command injection vulnerability with a score of 8.6 and affects six product families. Barracuda labels both vulnerabilities “High” in its advisory, despite the first flaw’s 9.3 score. The first weakness concerns authorization controls, while the second involves command injection. Barracuda says the combined attack could bypass those controls and obtain root access. However, the advisory does not publish vulnerable endpoints, example requests, payloads, or a detailed exploit sequence. Administrators should therefore avoid treating an assumed attack chain as confirmed technical evidence. Earlier coverage of Barracuda gateway command injection explains how a separate flaw, CVE-2023-2868, enabled system command execution through malicious archive processing. That historical vulnerability is not one of the newly disclosed issues, and its exploitation method should not be applied to this advisory. An important limitation remains unresolved in the published details. Barracuda calls CVE-2026-116606 a pre-authentication authorization bypass, yet its advisory also lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.” Its overview states that attackers need access to the administrative interface. These statements do not clearly establish whether valid administrator credentials are required for every exploitation scenario. Only ESG is listed as affected by both vulnerabilities. The command injection flaw also affects Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway. The published matrix does not list those five additional products as vulnerable to the authorization bypass. The broader concern is familiar: security appliances can become valuable entry points when exploitable weaknesses remain exposed. Reporting on most exploited security vulnerabilities previously included Barracuda ESG among products targeted through known flaws. That history provides context for patching urgency, but it does not establish exploitation of these newly disclosed CVEs. Patches, Administrative Exposure, and Defensive Priorities Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls. Organizations whose management interfaces are not publicly accessible face less exposure to this attack path. Reducing internet exposure is therefore an immediate containment measure, but the vendor still directs customers to update firmware and apply all security patches. The supplied advisory lists ESG patches BNSF-40425 for versions 9.4.017 and later, and BNSF-40430 for earlier versions. It identifies BNADC-16586 for ADC and WAF, BNMA-32468 for Message Archiver, BNWF-60060 for WAF Control Center, and BNYF-24789 for Web Security Gateway. These identifiers help administrators verify remediation against the affected product. Customers should check the latest firmware offered by each appliance and confirm that patches actually installed. Systems several firmware versions behind may require multiple updates. If automatic patching did not apply an update, Barracuda advises installing it manually as soon as possible and enabling automatic patch delivery where it has been disabled. Previous reporting on network device root access illustrates why management interfaces deserve close attention during vulnerability response. For this disclosure, however, administrators should follow Barracuda’s product-specific guidance rather than assume another vendor’s exploit methods or recovery requirements apply. Barracuda Support can help verify firmware and patch status. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, were disclosed on November 2, 2026. Barracuda has released patches and urged customers to install the latest firmware and verify that security updates have reached their devices.

Its advisory does not report active exploitation or identify an associated attack campaign. Barracuda researchers identified the vulnerabilities, not a malware strain.

The distinction matters because the disclosure describes weaknesses in appliance access controls and command handling rather than a documented malware infection.

According to the official Barracuda security advisory, combining these weaknesses could give an attacker root access to an affected device.

Critical Barracuda Security Flaws

CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorization bypass affecting Barracuda Email Security Gateway, commonly called ESG.

It carries a CVSS score of 9.3. CVE-2026-111560 is a command injection vulnerability with a score of 8.6 and affects six product families. Barracuda labels both vulnerabilities “High” in its advisory, despite the first flaw’s 9.3 score.

The first weakness concerns authorization controls, while the second involves command injection. Barracuda says the combined attack could bypass those controls and obtain root access.

However, the advisory does not publish vulnerable endpoints, example requests, payloads, or a detailed exploit sequence. Administrators should therefore avoid treating an assumed attack chain as confirmed technical evidence.

Earlier coverage of Barracuda gateway command injection explains how a separate flaw, CVE-2023-2868, enabled system command execution through malicious archive processing.

That historical vulnerability is not one of the newly disclosed issues, and its exploitation method should not be applied to this advisory.

An important limitation remains unresolved in the published details. Barracuda calls CVE-2026-116606 a pre-authentication authorization bypass, yet its advisory also lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.”

Its overview states that attackers need access to the administrative interface. These statements do not clearly establish whether valid administrator credentials are required for every exploitation scenario.

Only ESG is listed as affected by both vulnerabilities. The command injection flaw also affects Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway.

The published matrix does not list those five additional products as vulnerable to the authorization bypass. The broader concern is familiar: security appliances can become valuable entry points when exploitable weaknesses remain exposed.

Reporting on most exploited security vulnerabilities previously included Barracuda ESG among products targeted through known flaws. That history provides context for patching urgency, but it does not establish exploitation of these newly disclosed CVEs.

Patches, Administrative Exposure, and Defensive Priorities

Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls. Organizations whose management interfaces are not publicly accessible face less exposure to this attack path.

Reducing internet exposure is therefore an immediate containment measure, but the vendor still directs customers to update firmware and apply all security patches.

The supplied advisory lists ESG patches BNSF-40425 for versions 9.4.017 and later, and BNSF-40430 for earlier versions.

It identifies BNADC-16586 for ADC and WAF, BNMA-32468 for Message Archiver, BNWF-60060 for WAF Control Center, and BNYF-24789 for Web Security Gateway. These identifiers help administrators verify remediation against the affected product.

Customers should check the latest firmware offered by each appliance and confirm that patches actually installed. Systems several firmware versions behind may require multiple updates.

If automatic patching did not apply an update, Barracuda advises installing it manually as soon as possible and enabling automatic patch delivery where it has been disabled.

Previous reporting on network device root access illustrates why management interfaces deserve close attention during vulnerability response.

For this disclosure, however, administrators should follow Barracuda’s product-specific guidance rather than assume another vendor’s exploit methods or recovery requirements apply. Barracuda Support can help verify firmware and patch status.

items.title: Node.js Schedules High-Severity Security Fixes for 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x Release Lines
items.summary: The Node.js project has scheduled security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines on or shortly after Wednesday, November 11, 2026. The announcement gives developers and system administrators time to prepare for patches addressing HIGH-rated vulnerabilities across all three branches. Each release line will receive a fix for at least one high-severity issue. However, the advance notice does not list vulnerability counts, CVE identifiers, affected components, or fixed version numbers. It also provides no details about attack methods or confirmed exploitation, leaving the exact technical risk unclear until further information becomes available. The planned updates follow earlier Node.js security fixes covering TLS, DNS, and Brotli . Those October patches addressed separate weaknesses in certificate checks, name resolution, and compressed data handling. Node2Shell Adds Concern One notable October issue was Node2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 , a high-severity flaw in Node.js’s bundled Brotli decoder. It affected the same three release lines and could allow an attacker to corrupt process memory when an application decompressed malicious Brotli data through the node:zlib module. The decoder incorrectly treated an invalid block switch as a request for more input rather than a permanent error. It then continued adding bytes beyond an eight-byte internal buffer. Depending on application behavior, this could cause a crash, expose process memory, or allow remote code execution. According to the official October advisory , Node2Shell was addressed in that earlier security release. Fixes shipped in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. It should therefore be treated as separate background, not described as a confirmed vulnerability in November’s planned patch set. Supported Versions and Older Releases Node.js also warns that end-of-life versions are affected when security releases occur. Running an older branch should therefore not be treated as protection simply because it is absent from the patch list. The project directs users toward an up-to-date, supported release rather than continued use of unsupported versions. The official release schedule lists Node.js 26.x as Active Long-Term Support, while 24.x and 22.x are in Maintenance support. Maintenance branches still receive security updates. Earlier coverage of Node.js security flaws affecting supported branches shows why teams must track runtime updates alongside application changes. According to the official security advisory , November 11 is a target rather than a guaranteed publication deadline. Teams should monitor the notice for release availability and technical details. Until those details arrive, claims about remote code execution, data theft, or specific workarounds would go beyond the published information. For deployment planning, the Node.js release schedule provides the support status and end-of-life dates for each branch. The immediate priority is identifying which release lines applications use and preparing to test the forthcoming updates. Organizations on unsupported versions should plan migration to a supported branch rather than expect patches for retired releases. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
items.summary: On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux . It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google. Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38 . It will become available on Google Play over the coming days. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . Technical details Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look. Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page. items.title: OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers
items.summary: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell , started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project , is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem : Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process : before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network : outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials : the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox , the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster. A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart. How a sandbox is created and run On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail. Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue ( openshell/#1719 ) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator. Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018 ). OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back. OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. Which images run, how big a sandbox can get, which credentials it gets, and who can change OpenShell’s RBAC are left to the platform team. OpenShell vs. Agent Substrate Agent Substrate is another CNCF project that provides sandboxed execution for agents. Both projects applied, and were accepted, to the CNCF Sandbox in September, 2026 ( #522 and #523 ). Both run each agent in its own sandbox on Kubernetes, but they are built differently. OpenShell uses the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project. Substrate has its own scheduler, controller, and sandbox runtime. Lin Sun’s CNCF post, Why sandboxing your agent is not enough , makes the case for Substrate: “Sandboxing your agents is necessary, but not sufficient.” Agent Sandbox is about running agents securely. Substrate is about running them securely and cheaply at scale, by suspending idle agents instead of giving each one a Pod. Agent Substrate is not meant to be used directly, but requires an orchestration layer like Agent Executor , Kagent, or possibly in the future OpenShell (more on that below). OpenShell Agent Substrate Origin NVIDIA Google CNCF Sandbox Voted in Sep 26, 2026 Voted in Sep 28, 2026 Main problem What may this agent do? How do we run thousands of mostly idle agents cheaply? Unit of work One sandbox per agent: a Sandbox, a workload Pod, and a supervisor Pod An actor: an identity plus a snapshot. When active, it runs in its own sandbox inside a shared worker Pod. Workers are designed to hold many actors (–max-actors defaults to 1,000), but the autoscaling demo notes that each worker holds one actor today Kubernetes building block Agent Sandbox. The gateway creates agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resources, and the Agent Sandbox controller reconciles them Its own WorkerPool CRD (ate.dev), which atecontroller turns into a Deployment of worker Pods. It does not use Agent Sandbox Routing Through the gateway and the sandbox’s supervisor An ate-target-actor header. The router resumes the actor if needed, and atunnel passes the request to its sandbox. Actors have no Pod IP Credentials The supervisor swaps a placeholder for the real key, only at endpoints the provider allows The egress gateway swaps an ate-secret:// placeholder header for the real credential. Actors and snapshots never hold the secret Identity Supervisor identity tied to the namespace, Sandbox UID, Pod UID, and runtime generation A SPIFFE X.509 certificate per actor, valid for 1 hour, and mTLS between all components. OpenFGA access policies are in progress State A /sandbox PVC that survives stop and start RAM and filesystem snapshots in object storage. Suspend and resume take under a second; the goal is 100 ms at p95 Autoscaling HPA for the gateway (more than one replica needs external PostgreSQL) and node autoscalers. Sandbox has no /scale subresource, so HPA, KEDA, and VPA cannot target a sandbox. Each new agent is a gateway API call WorkerPool has a /scale subresource, so HPA can scale workers on how full they are (the demo runs on kind only), plus node autoscalers. Requests wait when the pool is full Maturity v0.1.x Pre-1.0. Three areas that will matter most to Kubernetes cluster admins:: How detailed the policy is . OpenShell checks each request at a supervisor that serves one sandbox. It can let curl read GitHub issues and block curl from creating one. Substrate checks traffic at a shared egress gateway, per actor and per destination host. There is work underway to natively support OpenFGA policies and allow external policy. What Kubernetes can see . Each OpenShell sandbox is a set of Kubernetes objects, so RBAC, Kyverno, audit logs, and kubectl work on it. Substrate keeps actors, templates, and egress policies in its own API, backed by PostgreSQL, so the Kubernetes API server is not on the request path. Admission control sees Substrate’s worker pools, but not the agents or their egress policies. Isolation . Substrate requires a gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor sandbox for every actor; a plain container is not supported. That is what makes its snapshots possible. OpenShell runs a standard container with Landlock and seccomp, and you can require a stronger RuntimeClass for untrusted agents. Scaling follows from this. With OpenShell, your application decides how many sandboxes to run, and you size each one when you create it, as the demo does with Kyverno defaults and caps. With Substrate, HPA scales the worker pools, and the number of agents is separate from the number of Pods. For now, choose based on your workload. If you have many bursty, mostly idle agents, such as one assistant per user, and cost per agent matters most, look at Substrate. If your agents hold real credentials and reach production systems, and you need per-request control and policy on Kubernetes objects, look at OpenShell. Many large enterprises will likely need a mix eventually, and in the future, you may be able to use both. OpenShell’s RFC 0012 , merged Sep 10, 2026, makes isolation a pluggable isolation backend , separate from the supervisor that enforces policy. What OpenShell is

AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. 

OpenShell, started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project, is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML:

  • Filesystem: Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable.
  • Process: before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp.
  • Network: outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method.
  • Credentials: the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows.

For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox, the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster.

A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart.

How a sandbox is created and run

On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail.

Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue (openshell/#1719) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator.

Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018). 

OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path

The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission.

  1. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart.
  2. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs.
  3. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth.
  4. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state.
  5. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back.
  6. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails.
  7. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off.
  8. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed.
  9. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request.
  10. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back.

OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. Which images run, how big a sandbox can get, which credentials it gets, and who can change OpenShell’s RBAC are left to the platform team.

OpenShell vs. Agent Substrate

Agent Substrate is another CNCF project that provides sandboxed execution for agents. Both projects applied, and were accepted, to the CNCF Sandbox in September, 2026 (#522 and #523). Both run each agent in its own sandbox on Kubernetes, but they are built differently. OpenShell uses the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project. Substrate has its own scheduler, controller, and sandbox runtime.

Lin Sun’s CNCF post, Why sandboxing your agent is not enough, makes the case for Substrate: “Sandboxing your agents is necessary, but not sufficient.” Agent Sandbox is about running agents securely. Substrate is about running them securely and cheaply at scale, by suspending idle agents instead of giving each one a Pod. 

Agent Substrate is not meant to be used directly, but requires an orchestration layer like Agent Executor, Kagent, or possibly in the future OpenShell (more on that below).

Actors have no Pod IPCredentialsThe supervisor swaps a placeholder for the real key, only at endpoints the provider allowsThe egress gateway swaps an ate-secret:// placeholder header for the real credential. Sandbox has no /scale subresource, so HPA, KEDA, and VPA cannot target a sandbox. Each new agent is a gateway API callWorkerPool has a /scale subresource, so HPA can scale workers on how full they are (the demo runs on kind only), plus node autoscalers. Requests wait when the pool is fullMaturityv0.1.xPre-1.0. 

Three areas that will matter most to Kubernetes cluster admins::

  1. How detailed the policy is. OpenShell checks each request at a supervisor that serves one sandbox. It can let curl read GitHub issues and block curl from creating one. Substrate checks traffic at a shared egress gateway, per actor and per destination host. There is work underway to natively support OpenFGA policies and allow external policy.
  2. What Kubernetes can see. Each OpenShell sandbox is a set of Kubernetes objects, so RBAC, Kyverno, audit logs, and kubectl work on it. Substrate keeps actors, templates, and egress policies in its own API, backed by PostgreSQL, so the Kubernetes API server is not on the request path. Admission control sees Substrate’s worker pools, but not the agents or their egress policies.
  3. Isolation. Substrate requires a gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor sandbox for every actor; a plain container is not supported. That is what makes its snapshots possible. OpenShell runs a standard container with Landlock and seccomp, and you can require a stronger RuntimeClass for untrusted agents.

Scaling follows from this. With OpenShell, your application decides how many sandboxes to run, and you size each one when you create it, as the demo does with Kyverno defaults and caps. With Substrate, HPA scales the worker pools, and the number of agents is separate from the number of Pods.

For now, choose based on your workload. If you have many bursty, mostly idle agents, such as one assistant per user, and cost per agent matters most, look at Substrate. If your agents hold real credentials and reach production systems, and you need per-request control and policy on Kubernetes objects, look at OpenShell.

What Kyverno adds

items.title: Hackers Exploit Zyxel GS1900 Zero-Day in the Wild to Hijack Network Switches
items.summary: A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switches was already being used by hackers, and the patch meant to fix it did not work. Researchers at Binarly found that a public exploit hit a different bug than the one Zyxel had patched. Zyxel has now confirmed it as a new flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-107441. Zyxel published its fix for CVE-2026-7273 on June 16, 2026. After GreyNoise reported real attacks in September, Binarly tested all ten fixed firmware releases on September 28 and found every one still open. Zyxel confirmed the new bug on October 11, shipped a fix on October 22, and published its advisory on November 3. The flaw sits in the dispatcher.cgi web program. It carries a 9.8 critical score, and an attacker can run commands as root without logging in. The same weak code also exists in httprestorecfg.cgi and httpupload.cgi . Zyxel GS1900 Zero-Day Exploited The switch web page stores request parameters in a fixed memory block of 140 slots. Each slot holds 1,024 bytes. The code copies the data first and checks the count afterward. A long value in slot 139 spills over and overwrites the counter itself. An attacker can set the counter to a negative number and write to memory before the block. This lets them overwrite function pointers and run their own commands. Zyxel’s patch added a count check, but the bad copy still happens before that check runs. Binarly also says Zyxel described the bug wrongly. The flaw lives in global memory, not on the stack. It also works over normal HTTP from any network that can reach the switch, so Binarly rates it higher than the 8.8 score Zyxel gave. GreyNoise says one actor hit 996 GS1900 switches in 48 countries around August 17. The actor stole device settings, hashed root passwords, and network details. A total of 564 of those switches still used factory default logins. Italy, the United States, and Taiwan had the most victims. The exploit was a Python script hidden with PyArmor. It pulled a collector script from the attacker’s server using TFTP, then copied the stolen data to a web-readable folder. GreyNoise ties the actor to the Gitea campaign that Acronis called Red Heron , based on shared servers and malware. That campaign used JITTERLY, a Linux backdoor with more than 30 commands. It hides a rootkit called SIXZUT inside itself, which can conceal files, processes, and network links. Binarly found its samples while checking this server for Binarly Transparency Platform detections. CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on September 21. Our earlier report on the CISA warning for Zyxel GS1900 switches covers that step. Binarly now says either Zyxel’s first patch was wrong, or the attacks hit a different bug than CISA named. Either way, the flaw in Binarly’s advisory is present in the ten releases sold as fixes. The same actor also broke into WordPress sites, as our story on hackers exploiting WordPress flaws to steal government records shows. GreyNoise counted more than 18,000 stolen records in one case. Update every GS1900 switch to the October 22 fix or newer from Zyxel. Take web management pages off the internet and limit them to trusted admin networks. Change all default passwords right away. CISA also tells teams to check devices for odd admin activity, changed settings, and strange web requests. Because attackers took hashed root credentials, treat any exposed switch as possibly stolen and rotate its passwords. That campaign used JITTERLY, a Linux backdoor with more than 30 commands. It hides a rootkit called SIXZUT inside itself, which can conceal files, processes, and network links. Binarly found its samples while checking this server for Binarly Transparency Platform detections.

CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on September 21. Our earlier report on the CISA warning for Zyxel GS1900 switches covers that step. Binarly now says either Zyxel’s first patch was wrong, or the attacks hit a different bug than CISA named. Either way, the flaw in Binarly’s advisory is present in the ten releases sold as fixes.

The same actor also broke into WordPress sites, as our story on hackers exploiting WordPress flaws to steal government records shows. GreyNoise counted more than 18,000 stolen records in one case.

Update every GS1900 switch to the October 22 fix or newer from Zyxel. Take web management pages off the internet and limit them to trusted admin networks. Change all default passwords right away.

CISA also tells teams to check devices for odd admin activity, changed settings, and strange web requests. Because attackers took hashed root credentials, treat any exposed switch as possibly stolen and rotate its passwords.

Preserving user loyalty at the expense of half your wages is a bad trade. When a machine learning system does this, we call it "reward hacking." To avoid these perverse outcomes, programmers have to add more and more specificity to their objective functions: "speed run the game without teleporting or discovering an immortality hack." This explains a lot about the experience of watching a video on your phone. Any time you tune into a show on a streaming platform, you are forced to handle your phone with the delicacy of a photonegative. If any part of your hand brushes any part of the screen, you will immediately be whisked away from the video you're watching to an entirely different one: https://pluralistic.net/2022/05/15/the-fatfinger-economy/ Worse, after your program has been replaced with this new one, there's no obvious way to get back to the show you were just watching. Streaming video platforms are under enormous pressure to successfully recommend their back-catalog to their users, because the alternative (commissioning or purchasing a steady stream of popular new shows) is very expensive. Investors put a lot of stock in streaming services' "successful recommendation" rate. So streaming service bosses charge their product teams with making "successful recommendations." This is obvious reward hacking, so streaming bosses refined their objective function: they made their teams' bonuses contingent on getting you to watch a new video for a minimum time-frame. This in turn triggered the next volley in the reward-hacking wars, in which product teams took away the back button. This gives users any number of greased slides that whisk them away to a new video. To get back to the old video, users are forced to climb a greased pole. I recently switched from Android to Graphene, a de-googled phone operating system. Graphene's maintainers are blissfully free from the imperative to show that "users value AI features," and that's why I have never accidentally summoned up an undismissable AI by tapping a Graphene UI element. It's a different story when it comes to apps. Graphene has many different ways to install apps, including via Google Play (Google's default Android store). That's useful because it lets you install your old Android apps after switching to Graphene, but it does leave you exposed to the fatfinger economy. I make extensive use of an app called "Genius Scanner," which lets me scan receipts and email them to myself (I do this a lot because, as a freelancer, I have to track a lot of different expenses). I bought a lifetime subscription to Genius Scanner in 2023, after getting burned by Camscanner (my previous, now enshittified scanning app), and I've been perfectly happy with it…until now. I have seen that ad about 100 times at this point, because I keep tapping the spot where the "x" used to be. I'm certain that the company knew that its paying customers relied on the "x" to accomplish a vital function in any scanning app (giving good, descriptive titles to scans). items.title: Microsoft Edge Now Automatically Blocks Malicious Websites Sending Fake Virus Alert Notifications
items.summary: Microsoft Edge now automatically disables notifications from websites that send users to detected scam pages, cutting off a route used to deliver fake virus warnings. The protection connects Microsoft Defender SmartScreen and Scareware blocker detections with notification permissions, helping prevent malicious sites from repeatedly drawing people back into the same scam. The change arrived with Edge 156, according to Microsoft’s November 2 disclosure. Rather than simply warning about a dangerous destination, Edge can now stop further notifications from the website responsible for sending the user there. That distinction matters because closing a deceptive page does not necessarily stop notifications the visitor previously allowed. Researchers writing on Windows Blogs, Rob Franco and Lu Huang, noted the malicious notification abuse while reviewing user reports submitted through Scareware blocker. Their findings describe a recurring scam delivery method, not a newly named malware family: website notifications repeatedly brought users back to pages that Edge’s security tools identified as scams. Microsoft Edge Now Automatically Blocks Malicious Websites The attack starts with a permission request. A misleading website persuades someone to select “Allow,” sometimes claiming this is necessary to prove they are not a robot. That click grants notification access, giving the site repeated opportunities to display false security messages even after the original page has closed. These alerts borrow the language of antivirus products to create urgency. Related reporting on fake Microsoft security scans shows how convincing branding and fabricated findings can pressure users into unsafe decisions. Say yes once and fake alerts can start piling up (Source – Windows) A notification claiming that a computer is infected should therefore not be confused with a verified diagnosis from installed security software. Edge’s new response follows a specific detection chain. When Microsoft Defender SmartScreen or Scareware blocker identifies a scam reached through a notification, the browser automatically disables notifications from the originating site. This closes the route used to bring the user back, rather than addressing only the page currently open. The scope is important: Microsoft describes notification blocking tied to detected scams, not a guarantee that every deceptive website will be stopped before interaction. On the next browser launch, an information bar explains the action. Users can review blocked sites in Edge Settings and restore notifications if they believe the browser made an incorrect decision. The wider scam ecosystem explains why stopping repeat contact matters. Campaigns using the browser locking CypherLoc kit have combined full-screen warnings, hidden controls and alarming sounds to push fake Microsoft support calls. Those techniques are separate from notification permissions, but both depend on making a browser message look like a serious system emergency. Microsoft says Scareware blocker directly protects tens of thousands of users daily against new scams. Reports also support wider SmartScreen protection; during the preview, each report helped protect another 50 users. The new notification control extends that feedback process by acting on the delivery source as well as the destination. Reporting Suspicious Prompts and Stopping Repeat Scams Edge also offers a “Block and report” option within notification permission requests. Users can open the menu beside “Block” and report the requesting site before granting access. Reports can include the URL and a screenshot of the page that tried to persuade the visitor to enable notifications. This gives SmartScreen evidence earlier in the process, potentially before an abusive notification reaches anyone. The distinction between delivery and deception is also visible in malicious Google Ads campaigns that lead visitors to fake security warnings. Different entry points can feed similar support scams, making the original source worth investigating alongside the warning itself. The settings page lists the blocked site and lets you unblock to restore its notifications (Source – Windows) Users retain a manual way to stop unwanted messages when automatic detection does not intervene. Microsoft advises opening the “…” menu on a website notification and disabling future notifications from that site. Other buttons inside a fake alert may simply open more pop-up windows, so interacting with its supposed repair controls can prolong the scam. For security teams, the practical value is a shorter repeat-exposure window. Blocking a detected destination helps with one encounter; withdrawing the sender’s notification access also interrupts future attempts from that source. Microsoft describes the broader approach as connecting browser-side detection, user reports and cloud reputation to turn individual observations into protection for more users. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator type Source disclosure Malicious domains, URLs and IP addresses Not provided SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 hashes Not provided Named malware family Not identified Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly.
