items.title: Google Releases Major Chrome Security Update Fixing 213 Bugs, Including 7 Critical Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Google has released Chrome 157 for Windows, macOS, and Linux, fixing 213 security bugs, including seven rated critical. Announced on November 3, 2026, the update addresses flaws across graphics, memory handling, browser features, and access controls. Google says the stable release will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The patched versions are 157.0.8103.38 for Linux and 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and macOS. The release follows another large patch cycle covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on Chrome 156 fixing 353 security flaws , showing the continued need to keep browser updates current. Seven Critical Flaws Affect Memory Safety Two critical vulnerabilities involve buffer overflows in Dawn, Chrome’s implementation of the WebGPU graphics standard. CVE-2026-121156 was reported by Zhenpeng “Leo” Lin at depthfirst on September 30, earning a $10,000 reward. Google reported the second Dawn flaw, CVE-2026-121247, on October 3. A buffer overflow happens when software writes beyond the memory space set aside for data. Another critical issue, CVE-2026-121229, involves memory corruption in ANGLE. Researcher @mfx reported it on September 17 and received $1,000. Graphics-related security flaws have appeared in earlier releases, including the Chrome update fixing critical WebGL and Dawn vulnerabilities . These repeated fixes make graphics components an important area for browser security work. The remaining four critical bugs are use-after-free flaws. They affect WebGL through CVE-2026-121246, Prerender through CVE-2026-121035, Geometry through CVE-2026-121203, and Core through CVE-2026-121126. This type of flaw occurs when software keeps using memory after it has been released. Depending on the circumstances, attackers may manipulate that memory, although the release notes do not explain specific attack methods. Google’s official Chrome release announcement credits its own researchers for the WebGL issue. Xinyang Ge reported the Prerender and Geometry flaws, while Wenbin Liu reported the Core vulnerability. The Prerender entry specifically credits Ge at Anthropic, assisted by Claude. That credit documents AI-assisted research, but does not establish that the finding was fully automated. The update also patches high-severity issues beyond those seven critical bugs. These include incorrect authorization in BackgroundFetch, out-of-bounds memory access in ANGLE, type confusion in V8, and memory flaws in PDFium, Media, and other components. This wider coverage matters because browser security depends on many connected systems, not just the code that displays web pages. Google has not stated in this announcement that these vulnerabilities are being used in active attacks. It also does not provide proof-of-concept exploits or detailed attack chains. Readers should therefore distinguish the confirmed severity ratings from claims of confirmed code execution, sandbox escape, or complete device compromise. Those outcomes are not established by the published advisory. Users and IT teams should prioritize installing the patched release and confirming that browsers actually run the updated version. Google is keeping some technical details restricted until most users receive fixes. Restrictions may remain longer when shared third-party libraries are affected. The Chromium Security page explains its coordinated disclosure process and why access to sensitive bug information is limited. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Detection Engineering: Implementing Detection-as-Code in an Existing Environment: Part 2 – Execution
items.summary: In Part 1, we described the starting position and roadmap for introducing Detection-as-Code in an existing environment, this second part explains how we executed that roadmap. Some of the content in this part of the series is rather technical. If you are not a technical reader, feel free to skim this part, but do not miss Part 3, which returns to conceptual and strategic topics. Preparation The documents associated with a detection, but not directly part of its implementation, were intended to be machine-readable. In practice, however, many were not. The issues ranged from character-encoding problems and indentation errors to random null bytes in files. Furthermore, some files did not comply with the intended schema because keys were missing or incorrect. This did not cause significant problems in the old process. The documents were written, sometimes in plain-text editors without syntax highlighting, placed on file shares, and left there. In the new setup, however, the repository was intended to become the central single source of truth. All documents therefore needed to be parseable so that their correctness could be validated. Their contents were also required to execute the migration; for example, the metadata documents contained paths to the Atomic Red Team tests. To systematically correct these documents, we implemented a parsing library containing functions to read the different file types, validate them against a defined schema using strictyaml and jsonschema , and return the parsed results. These functions were used throughout the migration and later in automations. Using these parsers, we attempted to parse all files and identified issues requiring correction. While some issues could be addressed semi-automatically with scripts, for example by identifying and converting encodings, many had to be corrected manually, file by file. Because the existing deployment procedures required detection data in platform-specific formats, we needed tooling to generate those formats. For Splunk, this meant an apps directory that could be copied to the Splunk infrastructure. For Splunk, the process was relatively straightforward. The configuration files for a Splunk app, namely savedsearches.conf , transforms.conf , and macros.conf , could be created by concatenating the corresponding snippets, splunk-searches.conf , splunk-transforms.conf , and splunk-macros.conf , from all active detections assigned to a specific app. Lookup files were copied unchanged to the lookups folder of the relevant app. In the customer environment, Splunk detections were distributed across different Splunk apps based on their categories. The deployment script therefore iterated through all detection folders in the new repository, determined the target app from the data in meta.yml , and added the relevant configuration snippets and files to that app. Folders containing detections targeting platforms other than Splunk were skipped. Deployment scripts for the other platforms were created in the same way. They used the new detection repository as input and, without requiring additional parameters, generated the artefacts expected by the existing deployment processes. We also created a script for Atomic Red Team tests because the framework expects each test to be stored in a separate folder with a specific name. The script built the required path from information in meta.yml and copied the contents of each test file to the required location. After preparing the current data for the migration and the tooling required to continue deployment after the migration, the next step was to focus on the migration itself. The migration was scripted using Jupyter notebooks, which used the previously implemented parsers and operating-system libraries to copy, move, and edit files. The detailed migration process is covered in the next section. With the scripted migration and the CLI tools, we performed multiple dry runs. For each dry run, we executed the migration locally on a copy of all data and used the developed CLI tools to regenerate the deployment artefacts, which were expected to match the current data structure. Comparing the generated artefacts with the pre-migration data enabled us to identify and fix open issues, such as incorrect filenames or references in metadata files, until the generated artefacts matched the initial input. Lastly, before starting the short repository freeze and executing the migration in production, we prioritised completing as many ongoing developments as possible and merging their feature branches into the main branch. This reduced the necessary cleanup work after the migration, as the migration covered only the main branches. Feature branches no longer matched the repository structure after the migration and therefore required their diffs to be migrated manually. Execution of the Data Restructuring Because some data had already been stored and tracked in Git repositories for some time, we wanted to preserve its history in full. We therefore needed to perform all moves in a way that Git could trace the history. Git does not store file moves directly; instead, it infers them by comparing file versions. We therefore structured the migration so that Git could recognise moved files rather than treat them as entirely new data. To achieve this, we split the changes into two steps: one that left filenames and paths unchanged while changing only file content, and another that moved or renamed files without changing their contents. This enabled Git to reconstruct the complete change history, and git blame could still show when a line was changed, even when the change had been made in the old structure. Moving all detection data into the new repository while retaining the old repositories for platform configuration required the histories of all repositories to be connected. For the restructuring, we used a local Git repository as an integration point before pushing the new content back to GitHub. Git allows branches from different repositories to be fetched and merged, even when they have no common history. We therefore added the old repositories as remotes, fetched the relevant branches, and brought their contents into the single local repository as unconnected trees. These branches could then be merged like any other branches in a Git repository. Because this setup is relatively uncommon, the Git CLI requires the ‑‑allow‑unrelated‑histories flag to confirm that the action is intentional. After all restructuring and Git operations, the local repository contained a branch with the new content for each repository. These branches were then pushed back to their respective remotes. Because each repository’s own history was included in the history of its new branch, we could push the result to the remotes without force-pushing. Where the main branch was protected, we pushed the result as a feature branch and merged it through a pull request on GitHub. The main branches of all repositories, as well as the file share, had to be frozen from the moment their data was pulled into the local repository and the file-share content was downloaded to the point at which the new contents had been pushed to the relevant repositories and approved through pull requests. Because the migration process was scripted and tested beforehand, the freeze period, including manual verification, could be kept to approximately half a day. With only the main branches frozen, development on feature branches continued during the migration. The full graph of the restructuring in the local repository is shown below. Each step is explained in the following paragraphs. Within the local repository, we started with a new empty main branch and initialised it with a README.md file explaining the structure of the new detection repository. We then started building the new structure by adding the metadata documents from the file share. For each detection, we created a folder based on the metadata and placed the document from the file share inside it as meta.yml . We then migrated the data from an existing Git repository. Starting from the tip of the main branch, we created two branches: one for the data to be moved to the new detection repository and another for the remaining data in the platform-specific repository. All data was distributed between these two branches so that, after the restructuring, each item existed in only one branch. In the branch for the detection repository, files were moved and renamed to match the target structure. As described earlier, we separated renames and content changes into different commits so that Git could reconstruct the history reliably. For the Splunk repository, we checked out both branches into adjacent working directories. We then removed the existing content from the working directory for the detection-repository branch. The migration script then iterated through the Splunk apps in the working directory for the platform-repository branch and processed their searches, transforms, macros, and lookup files. For each configuration block, the script attempted to identify the corresponding detection. In Part 1, we described the starting position and roadmap for introducing Detection-as-Code in an existing environment, this second part explains how we executed that roadmap.

Some of the content in this part of the series is rather technical. If you are not a technical reader, feel free to skim this part, but do not miss Part 3, which returns to conceptual and strategic topics.

Preparation

The documents associated with a detection, but not directly part of its implementation, were intended to be machine-readable. In practice, however, many were not. The issues ranged from character-encoding problems and indentation errors to random null bytes in files. Furthermore, some files did not comply with the intended schema because keys were missing or incorrect.

This did not cause significant problems in the old process. The documents were written, sometimes in plain-text editors without syntax highlighting, placed on file shares, and left there. In the new setup, however, the repository was intended to become the central single source of truth. All documents therefore needed to be parseable so that their correctness could be validated. Their contents were also required to execute the migration; for example, the metadata documents contained paths to the Atomic Red Team tests.

To systematically correct these documents, we implemented a parsing library containing functions to read the different file types, validate them against a defined schema using strictyaml and jsonschema, and return the parsed results. These functions were used throughout the migration and later in automations.

Using these parsers, we attempted to parse all files and identified issues requiring correction. While some issues could be addressed semi-automatically with scripts, for example by identifying and converting encodings, many had to be corrected manually, file by file.

Because the existing deployment procedures required detection data in platform-specific formats, we needed tooling to generate those formats. For Splunk, this meant an apps directory that could be copied to the Splunk infrastructure.

For Splunk, the process was relatively straightforward. The configuration files for a Splunk app, namely savedsearches.conf, transforms.conf, and macros.conf, could be created by concatenating the corresponding snippets, splunk-searches.conf, splunk-transforms.conf, and splunk-macros.conf, from all active detections assigned to a specific app. Lookup files were copied unchanged to the lookups folder of the relevant app.

In the customer environment, Splunk detections were distributed across different Splunk apps based on their categories. The deployment script therefore iterated through all detection folders in the new repository, determined the target app from the data in meta.yml, and added the relevant configuration snippets and files to that app. Folders containing detections targeting platforms other than Splunk were skipped.

Deployment scripts for the other platforms were created in the same way. They used the new detection repository as input and, without requiring additional parameters, generated the artefacts expected by the existing deployment processes.

We also created a script for Atomic Red Team tests because the framework expects each test to be stored in a separate folder with a specific name. The script built the required path from information in meta.yml and copied the contents of each test file to the required location.

After preparing the current data for the migration and the tooling required to continue deployment after the migration, the next step was to focus on the migration itself. The migration was scripted using Jupyter notebooks, which used the previously implemented parsers and operating-system libraries to copy, move, and edit files. The detailed migration process is covered in the next section.

With the scripted migration and the CLI tools, we performed multiple dry runs. For each dry run, we executed the migration locally on a copy of all data and used the developed CLI tools to regenerate the deployment artefacts, which were expected to match the current data structure. Comparing the generated artefacts with the pre-migration data enabled us to identify and fix open issues, such as incorrect filenames or references in metadata files, until the generated artefacts matched the initial input.

Lastly, before starting the short repository freeze and executing the migration in production, we prioritised completing as many ongoing developments as possible and merging their feature branches into the main branch. This reduced the necessary cleanup work after the migration, as the migration covered only the main branches. Feature branches no longer matched the repository structure after the migration and therefore required their diffs to be migrated manually.

Execution of the Data Restructuring

Because some data had already been stored and tracked in Git repositories for some time, we wanted to preserve its history in full. We therefore needed to perform all moves in a way that Git could trace the history. Git does not store file moves directly; instead, it infers them by comparing file versions. We therefore structured the migration so that Git could recognise moved files rather than treat them as entirely new data. To achieve this, we split the changes into two steps: one that left filenames and paths unchanged while changing only file content, and another that moved or renamed files without changing their contents. This enabled Git to reconstruct the complete change history, and git blame could still show when a line was changed, even when the change had been made in the old structure.

Moving all detection data into the new repository while retaining the old repositories for platform configuration required the histories of all repositories to be connected. For the restructuring, we used a local Git repository as an integration point before pushing the new content back to GitHub. Git allows branches from different repositories to be fetched and merged, even when they have no common history. We therefore added the old repositories as remotes, fetched the relevant branches, and brought their contents into the single local repository as unconnected trees. These branches could then be merged like any other branches in a Git repository. Because this setup is relatively uncommon, the Git CLI requires the ‑‑allow‑unrelated‑histories flag to confirm that the action is intentional. After all restructuring and Git operations, the local repository contained a branch with the new content for each repository. These branches were then pushed back to their respective remotes.

Because each repository’s own history was included in the history of its new branch, we could push the result to the remotes without force-pushing. Where the main branch was protected, we pushed the result as a feature branch and merged it through a pull request on GitHub.

The main branches of all repositories, as well as the file share, had to be frozen from the moment their data was pulled into the local repository and the file-share content was downloaded to the point at which the new contents had been pushed to the relevant repositories and approved through pull requests. Because the migration process was scripted and tested beforehand, the freeze period, including manual verification, could be kept to approximately half a day. With only the main branches frozen, development on feature branches continued during the migration.

The full graph of the restructuring in the local repository is shown below. Each step is explained in the following paragraphs.

Within the local repository, we started with a new empty main branch and initialised it with a README.md file explaining the structure of the new detection repository. We then started building the new structure by adding the metadata documents from the file share. For each detection, we created a folder based on the metadata and placed the document from the file share inside it as meta.yml.

We then migrated the data from an existing Git repository. Starting from the tip of the main branch, we created two branches: one for the data to be moved to the new detection repository and another for the remaining data in the platform-specific repository. All data was distributed between these two branches so that, after the restructuring, each item existed in only one branch. In the branch for the detection repository, files were moved and renamed to match the target structure. As described earlier, we separated renames and content changes into different commits so that Git could reconstruct the history reliably.

For the Splunk repository, we checked out both branches into adjacent working directories. We then removed the existing content from the working directory for the detection-repository branch. The migration script then iterated through the Splunk apps in the working directory for the platform-repository branch and processed their searches, transforms, macros, and lookup files.

For each configuration block, the script attempted to identify the corresponding detection. When a match was found, it removed the block from the source configuration file and moved it to the matching detection folder in the other working directory. For transforms, the associated lookup file was moved together with the configuration block. To preserve the Git history of these moves, we used two commits. First, we copied the complete original configuration file, such as savedsearches.conf, to the target detection folder. After committing this copy, we removed the full file and added only the configuration blocks relevant to the detection in a separate commit. This left Git with sufficient similarity between the old and new files to recognise the move, even though most of the original file had been removed.

The Splunk repository also contained Atomic Red Team test scripts that had to be moved as part of the migration. However, test cases in these files did not follow a sufficiently consistent naming scheme to match them reliably to individual detections. Because the tests were used only manually during development, a complete matching of test cases to detections was not required for the initial restructuring. Instead, we copied each test script unchanged into the folder of every detection associated with the relevant MITRE ATT&CK technique. The resulting duplication was addressed during the post-restructuring cleanup described later.

After moving the data for the detection repository into its working directory and committing the changes in stages, this branch was ready to be merged. Because the main branch, which already contained the metadata documents, and the migration branch both already followed the target structure, the branches could be merged cleanly.

In the working directory for the platform-repository branch, the Splunk app folders then contained only configuration snippets that could not be matched to a detection. In our project, this included two transforms belonging to detections that had already been deleted but whose transforms had been overlooked. We pushed this branch to the original Splunk repository and merged it into the main branch through a pull request.

Restructuring the platform repository itself was outside the scope of the project. However, because it is now maintained solely by the Splunk platform team, a later overhaul can be performed without requiring coordination with the detection engineers.

After migrating the Splunk repository, we followed a similar procedure for the repositories containing data for the other detection platforms.

Post-Restructuring Cleanup

During the restructuring, only the main branches were frozen and development on feature branches continued. However, as these feature branches still had the old structure, the work could no longer be merged. These developments had to be recreated as feature branches in the new repository, after which the old branches could be closed without merging.

A developer working on a detection could continue working on the existing feature branch until it was ready for review. Once ready, the changes had to be moved to the detection repository. In this case, we used the diff shown in the GitHub pull request, which was more efficient than automating cherry-picks or another migration mechanism, and manually recreated the changes on a new feature branch in the detection repository. We then opened a new pull request for review, linked it to the old pull request where relevant context already existed, and closed the old pull request without merging.

The complete Atomic Red Team test script was copied into the folder of every detection covering the same MITRE ATT&CK technique. While this was a reasonable decision to enable the restructuring to proceed, it was not acceptable as a long-term solution. For each detection, all test cases belonging to other detections had to be removed from the test script. Fortunately, this could be partially automated because many test cases roughly followed a naming scheme that referenced the specific detection. The remaining test cases required manual investigation to assign them to a detection and retain them only within that detection.

Migration of remaining distributed data

At this point, all data originating from the file share and the different Git repositories had been organised in the new structure. To fully achieve the original goal of consolidating all detection-related data in GitHub, the final step was to address the data still stored in Excel reports.

Because the Excel reports are required for internal and regulatory processes, they must continue to exist and be kept up to date. However, after the migration, they were generated and updated from the data in GitHub, removing the need for manual edits.

Most of the data in the reports was already present in the metadata documents for the detections. For the additional data in the reports, we extended the metadata schema with the required fields. Afterwards, a script converted the metadata documents to the new schema, and the additional data from the Excel reports was added in a pull request.

In parallel, we developed CLI tools that parse the metadata documents and populate or update the existing Excel reports with data from the repository. This allows up-to-date reports to be generated at any time without manual editing; they always contain the most recent data from GitHub as the single source of truth.

Wrapping Up

We achieved two of the three main goals defined in Part 1.

First, we restructured the existing data to reflect the semantic structure of detections and the way developers interact with them, rather than the structure imposed by the detection platforms. Second, we successfully consolidated all detection-related data in GitHub. No detection-related data remained scattered across different locations. With GitHub as the central source of truth, information could be found easily and changes could be tracked cleanly.

The third goal, improving data quality and building on the new foundation with further automation, is the focus of Part 3. There, we will show how we identified and addressed data-quality issues, the measures taken to maintain a high-quality dataset over time, and the automations enabled by the new foundation.

items.summary: Ask a security team three questions. Is anyone trying to send customer data out of the company right now? Where does all of our customer data live today? And if a file with that data ends up on the wrong laptop next month, will it still be protected? Most teams can answer the first one. Some can answer the second. The third is the hardest, and it’s the one an auditor or a board member eventually asks. Data loss prevention (DLP) was built for the first question. Data security posture management (DSPM) was built for the second. In this post, I’ll walk through what each one does, where each one stops, and why I think a data security platform is the better way to answer all three. A quick note on words first. DLP and DSPM get used loosely, and a term can mean one thing to the vendor selling it and something else to the team buying it. So I’ll define each one plainly before comparing them. What DLP does Data loss prevention watches the ways data leaves your company. Email, web uploads, USB drives, cloud apps, and printers are the usual exits. When something that looks sensitive heads out, DLP can block it, warn the person sending it, or log it for review. It decides what’s sensitive by inspecting content against rules. A number that looks like a credit card. A document labeled confidential. Newer DLP tools add behavior signals and risk scoring, so fewer everyday actions get flagged as threats. Where DLP stops DLP works at the exits. It sees data at the moment someone tries to move it. It doesn’t tell you what’s sitting in a file share nobody has opened in five years, or how many copies of a customer spreadsheet exist across OneDrive, laptops, and cloud storage. It also can’t judge a file it can’t read. When an employee encrypts a file with a tool your company doesn’t manage, DLP can’t see inside it on the way out. That employee usually isn’t trying to get around your controls. They have a deadline and a file too sensitive to send in the clear, so they use whatever’s on the laptop. Then there’s tuning. Rules that are too strict bury analysts in alerts and stop people from doing their jobs. Rules that are too loose let real problems through. Keeping that balance is ongoing work for whoever owns the tool. What DSPM does Data security posture management answers a different question: what sensitive data do we have, where is it, and who can reach it? DSPM tools scan your data stores, classify what they find, and flag the risky spots. A storage bucket open to the internet. A folder of payroll records shared with the whole company. A copy of a customer database someone made for testing and forgot about. That inventory is valuable. You can’t protect data you don’t know you have, and the first thing an auditor asks is where your regulated data lives. Where DSPM stops DSPM is built to find and report. The fix usually goes somewhere else, often as a ticket in another team’s queue. Without follow-through, you end up with a dated list of problems. It proves you knew about them and does nothing to show you fixed them. Coverage is the other gap. Most DSPM tools started in the cloud and SaaS apps. Sensitive data also lives on laptops, on file servers in your own data center, and at many banks, insurers, and retailers, on the mainframe. A map that leaves those out only shows part of the house. Why DLP and DSPM are merging Run both tools side by side and the overlap shows up fast. Each has its own definition of sensitive data, its own console, its own alerts, and its own person keeping it running. The DSPM report says a folder is exposed. The DLP rule doesn’t know that. Nobody connects the two until something goes wrong. Data sprawl makes that gap wider every year. Customer records move between laptops, Microsoft 365, several clouds, and older core systems every day, and each tool sees only its slice. AI adds pressure. An AI assistant can open any file the person using it can open. If nobody knows which of those files hold customer data, nobody knows what the assistant might surface when someone types a prompt. And security teams are small. Every extra console is another rule set to maintain and another alert queue to work. That’s why vendors on both sides are building or buying the other half, and why buyers are asking for one platform instead of two tools. I think that’s a healthy shift. Nobody set out wanting two tools. They wanted to know where their sensitive data is and whether it’s protected, and two tools is how the market happened to sell the answer. What a data security platform does differently A data security platform treats finding data and protecting it as one job. It locates sensitive data wherever it lives, classifies it once under a single policy, and then acts on it. Encrypt it, mask it, redact it, quarantine it, or delete it. The finding and the fix happen in the same place. The bigger difference is where the protection lives. DLP guards the exits. DSPM watches the storage. A platform can put protection on the file itself, so it stays encrypted after it’s copied to a USB drive, attached to an email, or uploaded somewhere it shouldn’t be. If it lands in the wrong hands, what they have is unreadable. Take a simple example. An analyst exports a customer list to a spreadsheet on their laptop to build a quarterly report. With DLP alone, nothing happens until that file tries to leave. With DSPM alone, it shows up as a risk on the next scan, if the scan reaches laptops at all. With a platform, the file is found, classified, and encrypted where it sits. The analyst can still build the report, and if the file gets copied somewhere later, it stays protected. Capability DLP DSPM Data security platform The question it answers Is sensitive data leaving right now? What sensitive data do we have, and who can reach it? Where is our sensitive data, and is it protected wherever it goes? Where it works At the exits: email, web, USB, cloud apps In storage, mostly cloud and SaaS On endpoints, file servers, cloud, Microsoft 365, and core systems What happens when it finds a problem Blocks, warns, or logs the transfer Reports the risk, often as a ticket Encrypts, masks, redacts, quarantines, or deletes the data Where it’s strongest Stopping a specific transfer in the moment Building an inventory and spotting exposure Closing the gap between finding a problem and fixing it Where it’s weakest Data sitting still, and files it can’t read Fixing what it finds, and data outside the cloud Stopping a transfer mid-send. Protection on the file covers what happens after it leaves. That’s the case for one tool instead of two. When one policy decides what’s sensitive everywhere, and the same place that finds a problem also fixes it, there’s nothing to keep in sync between systems and no handoff for a problem to get lost in. Why this matters more in regulated industries At a bank, a health system, or an insurer, an auditor doesn’t want to hear that a tool flagged a problem. They want to know where regulated data lives, what you did about it, and whether it stayed protected. A list of findings with nothing done about them makes that conversation harder. The cost of getting it wrong is concrete. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report put the average U.S. breach at $10.22 million. And attackers don’t wait for a ticket queue. Incident response data from Unit 42 and the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report shows stolen data leaving in about 25 minutes from first access. No alert review or remediation ticket moves that fast. Protection that’s already on the file doesn’t have to. Why AI raises the stakes AI makes the discovery question urgent. Before you roll out an AI assistant, you need to know which files it can reach and whether the sensitive ones are protected. If customer data is exposed when AI arrives, the AI will find it. Getting your data found, classified, and protected is the step before AI, not the step after it. Six questions to ask before you buy 1 Can it find sensitive data on laptops, file servers, Microsoft 365, cloud storage, and the mainframe, or only in the cloud? 2 Does it use one classification policy everywhere, or a different one in each tool? 3 When it finds a problem, can it fix it on the spot, or does it open a ticket? 4 Does protection stay on the file after the file moves? 5 Can people still use protected data for their work, for testing, and for analytics? 6 Does it do all of this in one tool with one policy, or will you be stitching products together? Where PKWARE fits PK Protect is PKWARE’s data security platform, and it’s the product I own. It finds sensitive data on endpoints, in the cloud, in Microsoft 365, and on z/OS and IBM i mainframe systems, and applies one classification policy across all of them. From there, your team can encrypt, mask, redact, quarantine, or delete what it finds. Protection stays on the file after it moves, and format-preserving encryption keeps protected data usable for the systems and people that depend on it. We built PK Protect to find and fix in one place. Instead of a discovery tool and a separate protection tool, each with its own policy and console, your team gets one platform with one policy. That means clearer visibility into where sensitive data lives, less day-to-day work keeping tools running, fewer systems and processes to learn, and a lower total cost of ownership. If you want to know what’s sitting in your environment today, and whether it would still be protected tomorrow, the data exposure map takes about two minutes and asks four questions. Or reach out and I’m happy to talk it through with you.

Where it worksAt the exits: email, web, USB, cloud appsIn storage, mostly cloud and SaaSOn endpoints, file servers, cloud, Microsoft 365, and core systems What happens when it finds a problemBlocks, warns, or logs the transferReports the risk, often as a ticketEncrypts, masks, redacts, quarantines, or deletes the data Where it’s strongestStopping a specific transfer in the momentBuilding an inventory and spotting exposureClosing the gap between finding a problem and fixing it Where it’s weakestData sitting still, and files it can’t readFixing what it finds, and data outside the cloudStopping a transfer mid-send. Protection on the file covers what happens after it leaves.

That’s the case for one tool instead of two. When one policy decides what’s sensitive everywhere, and the same place that finds a problem also fixes it, there’s nothing to keep in sync between systems and no handoff for a problem to get lost in.

Why this matters more in regulated industries

At a bank, a health system, or an insurer, an auditor doesn’t want to hear that a tool flagged a problem. They want to know where regulated data lives, what you did about it, and whether it stayed protected. A list of findings with nothing done about them makes that conversation harder.

The cost of getting it wrong is concrete. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report put the average U.S. breach at $10.22 million.

And attackers don’t wait for a ticket queue. Incident response data from Unit 42 and the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report shows stolen data leaving in about 25 minutes from first access. No alert review or remediation ticket moves that fast. Protection that’s already on the file doesn’t have to.

Why AI raises the stakes

AI makes the discovery question urgent. Before you roll out an AI assistant, you need to know which files it can reach and whether the sensitive ones are protected.

If customer data is exposed when AI arrives, the AI will find it. Getting your data found, classified, and protected is the step before AI, not the step after it.

Six questions to ask before you buy
1

Can it find sensitive data on laptops, file servers, Microsoft 365, cloud storage, and the mainframe, or only in the cloud?

2

Does it use one classification policy everywhere, or a different one in each tool?

3

When it finds a problem, can it fix it on the spot, or does it open a ticket?

4

Does protection stay on the file after the file moves?

5

Can people still use protected data for their work, for testing, and for analytics?

6

Does it do all of this in one tool with one policy, or will you be stitching products together?

Where PKWARE fits

PK Protect is PKWARE’s data security platform, and it’s the product I own. It finds sensitive data on endpoints, in the cloud, in Microsoft 365, and on z/OS and IBM i mainframe systems, and applies one classification policy across all of them.

From there, your team can encrypt, mask, redact, quarantine, or delete what it finds. Protection stays on the file after it moves, and format-preserving encryption keeps protected data usable for the systems and people that depend on it.

We built PK Protect to find and fix in one place. Instead of a discovery tool and a separate protection tool, each with its own policy and console, your team gets one platform with one policy.

That means clearer visibility into where sensitive data lives, less day-to-day work keeping tools running, fewer systems and processes to learn, and a lower total cost of ownership.

items.title: Hackers Use Stolen Microsoft Entra ID and Azure DevOps Credentials to Access 27 Organizations
items.summary: Hackers are abusing stolen Microsoft Entra ID application credentials and Azure DevOps identities to access Microsoft 365 and Azure environments, reaching at least 27 organizations. Todyl’s latest investigation update describes an ongoing campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) and their customers since November 1, 2026. The operator targeted about 45 app registrations across roughly 18 organizations, with more than 33 authenticating successfully. Downstream access expanded the victim count to government, energy, agriculture, transportation, construction, legal, education, and nonprofit organizations. These figures cover only environments sending logs to Todyl, so the actual reach could be wider. Investigators recorded searches across about 25 tenants, downloads of 81 files, and access to approximately 2,279 mailbox items. The latest reported attempt, at 21:31 UTC on November 3, was blocked. No Microsoft vulnerability was involved. Instead, the attacker used valid credentials to act as trusted applications. Attack Chain (Source: Todyl) This distinction matters because application identities operate without a user signing in. Their existing permissions can allow access without an MFA prompt, while user-focused Conditional Access policies do not govern app-only authentication. Cybersecurity News previously covered how stolen credentials and excessive permissions can turn limited access into broader exposure. The attacker also used an Azure DevOps federated workload identity and replayed user session tokens. How the attacker stole the original credentials remains unknown. Todyl found no evidence that a vendor platform was compromised, even though credentials belonging to trusted security integrations were among those abused. Attack Moves Through Cloud Environments According to Todyl’s investigation , the operator typically requests an Azure Resource Manager token, followed by tokens for Key Vault, Microsoft Graph, and Storage. This sequence gives investigators a useful pattern to hunt, particularly when previously unused applications begin authenticating shortly afterward. The latest update describes 29 wildcard Microsoft Graph searches followed by SharePoint downloads at roughly one file per second. Collected material included password lists, private keys, VPN profiles, backup credentials, and remote access settings. Such files could enable further attacks beyond Microsoft 365, where Todyl’s cloud logs provide limited visibility. MSP relationships increased the damage. One multi-tenant application reached 15 customer tenants in repeated loops of about 10 seconds. The broader risk resembles earlier reporting on compromised accounts reaching Azure DevOps and cloud resources , although that case involved a different intrusion. Scripted clients accounted for 95% of observed sign-ins, with bursts reaching 24 attempts in 10 seconds. However, long pauses and changing browser signatures suggest human control. Todyl describes automation, not confirmed self-spreading malware. AI involvement remains a low-confidence possibility, and the operator has not been identified. Defenders should review service-principal sign-ins and non-interactive user logs for 199.19.77.84, the confirmed source address. Failed attempts matter alongside successful ones. Todyl recommends blocking the exact address rather than its entire hosting network, where unrelated activity exists. Response should include disabling affected applications where needed, removing compromised credentials, revoking user sessions, and rotating secrets in accessible vaults and documents. Workload-specific Conditional Access has licensing and coverage limits, so user policies alone are insufficient. MSPs should also review delegated customer access, preserve audit logs, and notify affected clients. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Hackers Use OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit That Secretly Injects Ads Into AI Responses
items.summary: A jailbreak toolkit targeting OpenAI Codex is doing more than trying to bypass AI safety rules. The Chinese-language package, called Haiou, changes the coding agent’s trusted instructions so that ordinary greetings trigger advertisements for a third-party AI gateway. Researchers describe the behavior as prompt adware because it persists through written instructions rather than a conventional executable advertising payload. The discovery shows how installing an unofficial AI enhancement can change future responses without requiring a flaw in the underlying model. Haiou combines security-focused capabilities with promotional instructions, turning a tool marketed for unrestricted technical work into a distribution channel for its creator’s service. Its presence alongside hacking tools also shows that such packages have entered real cybercrime workflows. Check Point researchers identified the adware behavior while investigating a threat actor’s misconfigured webserver. Their November 3 technical report describes an exposed Cobalt Strike server whose logs showed compromises of private computers belonging to Chinese-speaking individuals. The server also hosted Ladon, VulnClaw, and Haiou. Researchers found no evidence connecting the jailbreak’s author to cybercrime, an important distinction between observed use and proven intent. Hackers Use OpenAI Codex Jailbreak Toolkit Check Point analyzed Haiou version 4.5.0, distributed through GitHub as a local Codex enhancement. Instead of exposing readable prompts throughout the repository, the package ships encrypted content. Its Windows, Linux, and macOS launchers verify Ed25519 signatures and SHA-256 hashes, then decrypt the payload using an embedded AES-256-GCM key before extracting a ZIP archive. That packaging makes casual inspection harder, although encryption alone does not prove malicious intent. The extracted material contains modular prompts and six security-related skills covering penetration testing, reverse engineering, license cracking, memory analysis, and game security. Like other prompt injection attack techniques affecting AI agents, Haiou relies on written instructions to redirect model behavior rather than exploiting a memory corruption vulnerability. Its jailbreak modules use role-playing, refusal suppression, and requests framed as educational capture-the-flag exercises. Other instructions discourage asking for authorization or setting boundaries before acting. Package contents (Source – Check Point) These are attempts to weaken safeguards; the report does not establish that every technique reliably bypasses every model or security restriction. The advertising rule sits inside the identity prompt module. When users enter specified greetings or activation words, the agent is told to return only a fixed promotional message. This resembles trigger activated prompt injection methods in which planted rules remain inactive until a matching condition appears, making a harmless greeting the entry point for an unwanted response. Another module labels the promoted gateway “protected infrastructure” and forbids offensive testing against it, even when users claim authorization. The package also includes an uninstaller that restores original configurations and removes the advertisement. These details show that persistence depends on installed agent instructions rather than an irreversible model change. AI Gateway Risks and Investigation Indicators The advertised service is an OpenAI-compatible gateway positioned between applications and model providers. Check Point found no indication that this particular gateway was malicious. Its assessment instead suggests that the freely available jailbreak likely helps attract customers to a paid service. The report does not establish credential theft, data theft, or malicious tool execution by this gateway. The wider concern is trust. Coverage of malicious AI marketplace skills has documented how agent extensions can influence recommendations and abuse trusted sessions. Haiou demonstrates a narrower outcome: persistent advertising through global instructions. Developers should therefore review prompt changes, installed skills, and gateway settings before trusting enhancement bundles, rather than treating readable instructions as harmless configuration. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Hackers Launch LLMHijacking Attacks, Leaving Companies With $1 Million in Cloud Bills
items.summary: Hackers are stealing access to corporate large language models and reselling it, leaving victims with cloud bills reaching $1 million. Mandiant investigated multiple incidents during 2026 where unauthorized AI use generated more than $100,000 in charges in a single day, showing how quickly stolen credentials can become a major financial loss. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) detailed the activity in research published November 2. The attacks affected financial services, retail, technology, and transportation organizations across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. Known as LLMJacking, the technique targets paid AI resources rather than using stolen computing power to mine cryptocurrency. The main entry point was exposed or stolen cloud credentials, including service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens, and active session tokens. Previous Cybersecurity News reporting on LLMjacking through a leaked AWS key describes a similar path from stolen access to unauthorized model use. Attackers also collected corporate LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories. To check whether keys worked without creating obvious traffic spikes, one group sent tiny requests using max_tokens=1 . These low-volume tests stayed below the victim’s security alert thresholds before larger abuse began. One tracked group, UNC6993, used a misconfigured service account key to reach cloud resources. It also operated a fake membership portal that persuaded users to paste session data containing active access tokens. Reusing those tokens allowed access without completing a fresh password or multifactor authentication check. Stolen AI Access Becomes a Resale Business According to Mandiant’s investigation , attackers increasingly split responsibilities. Some groups break into enterprise environments, while others run “LLM Mixers,” routing services that combine stolen credentials and sell unauthorized model access to paying subscribers. The victim receives the bill while the operators collect revenue. In one incident, an attacker made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours using stolen third-party keys. The activity powered Jet Night, a token-routing service that passed nearly $1 million in costs to one organization. GTIG believes its unusually cheap plans depend on stolen access. Credential theft is not the only concern. Attackers also searched private repositories, databases, and secret managers for additional passwords and keys. The risk mirrors concerns raised in Cybersecurity News coverage of the Northflank security incident , although that separate investigation has not established a link to these operations. Some intruders created administrator accounts, added SSH keys, and disguised backdoor service accounts as billing tools. In another case, Mandiant reported exploitation of LiteLLM flaw CVE-2026-40217 through /key/regenerate , allowing ordinary virtual keys to gain PROXY_ADMIN privileges and giving attackers lasting gateway control. The GTIG guidance urges defenders to treat unexpected activation of AI services as a critical warning. Several victims had not enabled LLM services before the intrusion. Teams should investigate new access keys, rapid account creation and deletion, unusual model requests, and attempts to disable logging. Organizations should rotate exposed secrets, restrict permissions, scan repositories for keys, patch gateways, and enforce model-specific quotas. Monitoring must include tiny validation requests, not just spending spikes. Revoking the first stolen key is insufficient when attackers have already created replacement accounts or other persistent access. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Hackers Hijacked French Blood Plasma Freezers, Changing Temperature Settings From −30°C to 110°C
items.summary: Hackers reportedly changed temperature settings on refrigeration equipment used by the French Blood Establishment, EFS, from around −30°C to 110°C after targeting its cooling service provider, Coolworld. The incident occurred overnight between November 1 and 2, 2026, raising concerns about frozen plasma stored for patient transfusions. According to reporting published by Cyberattaque citing Le Canard enchaîné, facilities in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté were among those concerned. France’s Health Ministry said staff detected the abnormal temperatures in time and that the incident caused no operational consequences. Coolworld supplies temperature-controlled equipment and maintenance services, including refrigerated containers used in medical settings. An on-call technician reportedly noticed temperatures rising during the night, allowing teams to respond before the disruption affected operations. Initial information concerned donor samples retained for blood safety monitoring. EFS later told Le Canard enchaîné that frozen plasma intended for transfusions was also involved. However, the available reports do not confirm destroyed plasma, disrupted transfusions, or harm to patients. The number of affected units, the length of the disruption, and the temperatures actually reached inside stored products remain undisclosed. No public technical findings identify the attackers or explain how they entered Coolworld’s systems, Cyberattaque reported . French Blood Plasma Freezers Hijacked The reported 110°C figure describes a setpoint, meaning the temperature requested through a control system. It does not establish that freezer interiors, blood samples, or plasma bags reached that temperature. Controller settings, measured air temperatures, and temperatures inside stored products are separate readings. This distinction matters because the risk depends on actual storage conditions and how long products remained outside approved limits. Reporting on the incident notes that fresh frozen plasma requires storage at −25°C or below. A prolonged temperature rise could make affected supplies unsuitable for transfusion. Investigators have not publicly identified a controller model, exploited vulnerability, or stolen maintenance account. Claims that a specific Danfoss flaw caused this incident would therefore go beyond the available evidence. The incident follows earlier attacks against supermarket refrigeration systems , where attackers reportedly changed settings to force continuous defrosting. Similar behavior does not prove that the same attackers, equipment, or entry method were involved at Coolworld. An October 12 CERT-FR security alert confirmed numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, alongside Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. The agency warned operators against exposing management interfaces directly to the internet. Cybersecurity News also documented internet-facing Danfoss systems , while noting that search results alone do not establish whether individual devices are vulnerable or compromised. No public evidence connects those exposed systems to the EFS incident. CERT-FR recommends removing public internet access, reviewing full device configurations, checking defrost schedules, and restoring remote access only through secure VPNs or protected networks. Supported equipment should receive firmware updates, default passwords must be changed, and applicable security settings should be enabled. For healthcare providers, the reported incident highlights risks extending beyond stolen records. A supplier compromise can affect equipment that preserves essential medical products. Independent temperature monitoring and prompt staff response were important safeguards here, although the full technical cause remains unknown. Available reporting contains no confirmed theft of donor information. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .
